Term by term: Varun, 0.30×4 + 0.25×3 + 0.20×3 + 0.15×5 + 0.10×4 = 1.20 + 0.75 + 0.60 + 0.75 + 0.40 = 3.70; Vivek, 0.90 + 1.00 + 1.00 + 0.45 + 0.30 = 3.65; Trupti, 0.90 + 0.75 + 0.40 + 0.75 + 0.40 = 3.20. The means in the last row are 19 / 5, 18 / 5 and 17 / 5.

The second-order effect is what matters. Varun beats Vivek by 3.80 − 3.60 = 0.20 unweighted but by only 3.70 − 3.65 = 0.05 weighted, because the scheme pays 30 per cent for product sense and 20 per cent for technical judgement; shift those weights and the ranking flips. Vedant's weights state which pivot risk his team can absorb: his line has three strong senior engineers and nobody who talks to customers, so he prices product sense high.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Claim 1: the pivot works when the target role's hardest problem is one the old job already solved. True for Varun: Vyavastha's yard product fails on customer discovery across sixteen mid-size manufacturers, a structured-interviewing problem he has run forty times. True for Urmila: Vihang's growth team fails on experiment design.

Claim 2: the pivot works when the organisation can absorb a ramp. Vyavastha has eleven product managers and a director who has run four transfers; it can, as can Vihang's growth pod. A six-person company cannot.

Claim 3: the evidence must be checkable by a stranger. Varun's strongest artefact was a written recommendation that a client not build a dealer portal, forecasting that fewer than one dealer in five would use it; eighteen months later a competitor shipped one and retired it. The document exists, dated, with his name on it. Urmila's equivalent: of eleven readouts, four said "do not ship" and all four were accepted.

The frame misleads in the over-evidenced pivot. Candidates with polished portfolios lose loops because their evidence is all of a kind they controlled: nobody disagreed with their side project, and the faculty under test is holding a position against opposition. The second misleading case is the senior transfer who treats the pivot as a title exchange, expecting group PM because the bands match. Bands are not scope, and the mismatch surfaces in month four.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Two-sided markets are the hardest pivot target. Tarini Freight Exchange, a Chennai marketplace matching shippers to truck fleets, finds that candidates from single-sided backgrounds reason about one side and treat the other as a constraint; its best pivots came from operations.

Regulated products add a constraint no instinct substitutes for. At Vishrut Insurance Services a PM cannot change policy wording without a filing cycle, and one who promises a customer a change in six weeks has created an incident. The tacit knowledge here is the regulator's tempo.

Hardware plus software widens the gap. At the Hyderabad GCC of Thornbury Instruments, where Vandana Thorat runs product for diagnostic analysers, a housing has a twenty-six-week tooling lead time against a two-week software sprint — a ratio of 26 / 2 = 13 to 1. Software-origin pivots plan as though it were 1 to 1, and the error is invisible until a tooling order slips.

AI-native products invert the usual advice. At Vimarsh Intelligence Works, a Bengaluru company building document-reasoning agents, behaviour is not specified but elicited, and the senior skill is designing evaluations. Analytics and research origins pivot in fastest, and the credential value of a long PM career is lowest here — which is why these are the most open door in India today.

Multi-product companies hire pivots into second-order products, where a slow ramp is contained; the practice is never stated, so a posting for a mature flagship should be read as requiring a prior PM title. Such companies also say they run one bar and run two: internal transfers judged on quarters of behaviour, external career-changers on four hours.

Exhibit 5. Internal transfers versus external career-changers, Vyavastha Systems, twenty-four months to 31 August 2026
RouteEntered processReached a loopOffersOffers per candidateIn the PM role at 18 months
Internal transfer96444.44%4 of 4 (100.0%)
External career-changer711857.04%3 of 5 (60.0%)

Internally, 4 / 9 = 44.44 per cent of candidates received an offer against 5 / 71 = 7.04 per cent externally, and 6 / 9 = 66.7 per cent reached a loop against 18 / 71 = 25.4 per cent. The ramp gap was starker. Weeks from start to the first roadmap decision the PM made alone and defended were 5, 7, 6 and 10 for the internal transfers — a sum of 28, mean 28 / 4 = 7.0 weeks — against 14, 11, 19, 13 and 16 for the external hires, a sum of 73, mean 73 / 5 = 14.6 weeks. The external mean is 14.6 / 7.0 = 2.09 times the internal one. The limit is plain: the rows are not the same cohort selected the same way, so the gap mixes selection with context.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The audit precedes the ambition. Competent candidates decide they want product management and then hunt for evidence. Experts run the inventory first — every decision in three years where they chose between options and lived with the result — and let it pick the target. The tell is the target: an expert's is narrow, a novice's a category.

A decision is not a task, and the difference is the rejected alternative. "I wrote the requirements and ran the standups" describes custody of a process; "I cut bulk upload, which three of our eight pilot customers wanted, because the two largest needed the audit trail first" describes a decision. The obvious reading — that interviewers want impact — is wrong; they want the counterfactual, the only observable trace of judgement.

Each origin's credibility gap has a different shape, and treating them as one gap is the commonest error. Engineers arrive with credibility inside the build team and a deficit on market judgement; sales and design arrive with the reverse.

The unlearning is specific and nameable. Consultants unlearn the complete answer: a deck that waits for full analysis is three sprints late. Engineers unlearn the solution-first reflex and false precision in estimates. Sales people unlearn treating the loudest account as the market; designers, owning the artefact rather than the trade-off; analysts, that a measurement is a decision; programme managers, that status is direction. The expert states their own item unprompted, which is itself the tell.

Seniority resets, and the only real question is the recovery period. Most pivots drop a band, and the expert negotiates not the drop but its duration: a written scope review at six months with named criteria, which is what Varun asked for. The obvious reading, that accepting a lower band signals weakness, is wrong; the manager reads it as someone who has priced the ramp honestly.

Internal pivots are won in the months before the posting exists. Urmila's panel was on 21 September, but her case was made across the eighteen months in which she wrote readouts saying "do not ship" and was believed. The competent candidate applies when the requisition opens; the expert has been doing fragments of the job, visibly, long before — and the tell is that their would-be manager has already quoted their work.

The MBA route compresses distribution, not evidence. A programme at ISB or an IIM buys campus access, a summer internship that is a legitimate product reference, and a cohort supplying referrals for a decade — which is what Exhibit 3's 329 / 2,350 = 14.00 per cent screen rate measures. What it does not buy is the audit. Candidates who treat the degree as evidence rather than channel reach loops and fail them.

A narrative that ends on the candidate has failed, however well told. Vedant is solving a portfolio problem, not ranking people, so the last sentence should name his problem rather than the candidate's ambition; experts ask early what the team is missing, and the question itself scores.

Interest in the role and fitness for it are different questions, and the loop tests only the second. Product work is sustained disagreement without authority, and someone who has never spent a week being told no by four stakeholders cannot know whether they want it. Experts shadow a PM before accepting; five days buys an option worth far more.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

Exhibit 6 gives median months from start date to first solo roadmap ownership across the career-changer hires Varnan placed in the same window — medians of separate cohorts, not totalled.

Exhibit 6. Median months to first solo roadmap ownership, career-changer hires
ContextMedian monthsOrigin most favoured
AI-native4Analytics, research
Consumer5Design, analytics
Marketplace6Operations
B2B software7Sales, engineering
Platform / internal tools9Engineering
Enterprise11Consulting
Hardware plus software13Programme, delivery

The spread is wide: the hardware median of 13 months is 13 / 4 = 3.25 times the AI-native median of 4. Stage pulls differently — at seed the pivot is easy to get and hard to survive, while from Series C onward and in the GCCs the internal route dominates. Where the difference is not real: the audit, the counterfactual and the checkability of evidence are identical in every cell.

8. Three worked examples

Urmila Virkar, analytics to APM, internal. Her central artefact was a checkout experiment that moved drop-off from 62.4 per cent to 57.9 per cent, a gain of 4.5 percentage points and a relative reduction of 4.5 / 62.4 = 7.21 per cent. The number got her the panel; what won it was a readout recommending against a referral incentive her skip-level wanted, on which she was overruled, and right. Tanushree Vispute, Vihang's vice-president of product, said that mattered more than the won experiment.

Vivek Thatte, design to PM, external. Hired by Tarini Freight Exchange in early 2026 after failing two loops, Vivek built his case on a carrier-onboarding redesign: on a base of 4,200 sign-ups a month, completion rose from 38 per cent to 51 per cent — from 4,200 × 0.38 = 1,596 completions to 4,200 × 0.51 = 2,142, a gain of 546 a month, or 546 / 1,596 = 34.21 per cent. The failures were instructive: both times he presented the design, not the trade-off. The third time he opened with the two things he had refused to change.

Trupti Uplekar, sales to PM: the failure and the recovery. Trupti joined Vishrut Insurance Services as a product manager on Monday 7 July 2025 and moved back to a commercial role on Monday 2 February 2026, thirty weeks later. The diagnosis was not capability. She had promised a broker a wording change in six weeks when the filing cycle was fourteen; the epic slipped fourteen weeks, and an initiative underwriting had valued at ₹120.00 lakh of annual retained premium arrived 14 / 52 of a year late, forgoing 14 / 52 × ₹120.00 lakh = ₹32.31 lakh of first-year value. Her replacement started on Monday 15 June 2026, leaving the seat empty nineteen weeks. Vishrut did not stop hiring from sales: it added a regulated-constraint exercise to the loop and paired every commercial-origin PM with a compliance lead for one filing cycle before they could commit a date externally. Trupti returned to product seven months later, in September 2026, at another insurer, the filing-cycle story now her strongest answer.

9. Failure modes, warning signs and the cost of a late catch

Exhibit 7. Four failure modes in a pivot
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of a late catch
Volume applyingScreen rate below 5% after 40 applicationsWhich had a person attached?Eight to twelve weeks
Task narrationNo rejected alternative in any storyWhat did I not do?Loops lost late
Solution-first reflexInterviewer hears architecture, not a choiceProblem stated first?Best screen rate wasted
Dates under constraintExternal commitment, no cycle checkWho must say yes?₹32.31 lakh, 19 weeks vacant

Every diagnostic above is cheap and available before the expensive stage: a minute in week two replaces a quarter lost in month nine.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position A: the only reliable pivot is internal. Steelmanned: product judgement is tacit and context-bound, so what predicts success is behaviour observed over quarters, not inference over hours. The evidence is Exhibit 5 — 4 of 4 internal transfers still in role at eighteen months against 3 of 5 external hires, and a mean ramp of 7.0 weeks against 14.6. It would be wrong if that advantage were mostly selection, which the exhibit cannot rule out, or if structured external loops closed the gap.

Position B: the ramp penalty is real but repaid with interest. Steelmanned: career-changers import scarce competences — a consultant's written synthesis, a designer's craft standard, an analyst's experimental discipline — and after the ramp raise the team's ceiling rather than filling a seat. It would be wrong if that competence decayed, or if these hires left before payback: a 2.09-times penalty needs tenure well beyond the ramp.

Position C: the MBA is the efficient Indian route and the industry under-admits it. Steelmanned: the binding constraint is distribution, not capability, and Exhibit 3's 14.00 per cent screen rate for consulting and MBA origins against 9.84 per cent overall is what a distribution advantage looks like. It would be wrong if that rate reflected selection into the programmes rather than their effect — and the data cannot separate the two.

Position D: a portfolio signals the wrong thing. Steelmanned: self-directed work shows initiative and craft but not judgement under opposition, the faculty being hired. It would be wrong if portfolios built inside the current employer, with named reviewers and real resistance, predicted success as well as prior PM experience — a measurable claim nobody has published.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves observably differently. They name a narrow target rather than a role, and answer "why product?" with a decision and its counterfactual rather than a motivation. They know their own unlearning item and say it before being asked. They ask what the team is missing before asking what the job pays, and negotiate the review date rather than the band. They can state the target business's regulatory, hardware or two-sided constraint in one sentence. And they distinguish the evidence that earns a screen from the evidence that earns an offer.

On the manager's side, mastery is publishing the weights and, when a hire fails, changing the loop rather than the origin.

12. The decisions

Varun Udeshi accepted Vyavastha's offer on Tuesday 6 October 2026, three days before it lapsed, having asked for and received a written scope review at six months. His reasoning was arithmetical: a ₹2.29 lakh gap, 5.87 per cent of ₹39.04 lakh, against a 14.6-week ramp he could now plan around. He accepted the band drop without argument, on the view that arguing it would signal the title-not-scope error he had learned to avoid.

Urmila Virkar was offered the associate PM role on Friday 9 October 2026 and accepted the same day. Her reasoning inverted Varun's: the internal route cost her nothing in pay — a rise of ₹3.35 lakh, 13.62 per cent — and bought a 7.0-week ramp among people who already believed her readouts. The cost was optionality: pivoting inside Vihang made her a PM at Vihang, and the external market would still ask for a title she would not hold for a year.

Discussion questions. First: Vedant Talpade's weights alone separate Varun's 3.70 from Vivek's 3.65. Is a weight scheme set by team composition a defensible instrument, or one that under-hires the competence a team has never had? Second: at what tenure does Exhibit 5's 2.09-times ramp penalty clear, and what would Vyavastha have to measure to know? Third: Vishrut answered Trupti Uplekar's failure by changing the loop rather than the origin it hired from. Under what evidence would changing the origin have been right?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does — decision rights determine the unlearning list; read it first. The career-switch narrative — turns the audit into the account a loop can test. A PM's operating system — what shortens Exhibit 5's ramp. Continuous learning as a PM — how Position B's payback arrives. PM interviews — the round structure Exhibit 4 implements. Building a PM portfolio and narrative — read against Position D. Your first 90 days in a PM role — where the two ramps are won. Confidence, doubt and judgement — calibrating certainty before earning it.
exp20v2-craft.transition:
Transitioning into Product Management

Lifecycle, Craft & Career › PM Craft, Productivity & Career. The question: coming from engineering, design, consulting or sales, what do I keep and what do I unlearn?

1. A Wednesday in April

On Wednesday 8 April 2026, Harshita Kamat, a senior engineer with nine years at Fulwari Software Services in Pune, received a written offer for a product manager role at Haveli Lending Works, a Bengaluru digital-lending company. The offer lapsed on Friday 17 April, nine days later. Its hiring manager, Gaurav Menezes, had told her plainly that she was the first engineer he had hired into product in two years, and that two other engineers on his shortlist had failed the final round.

The offer was a pay cut. Her current package was ₹47.52 lakh a year; Haveli's was ₹43.60 lakh. Staying also had a price: Fulwari had offered an internal move to associate product manager, at a reduced scope, if she waited for the next planning cycle. Her decision had a narrower core than it appeared. She was not choosing between two jobs. She was choosing whether a credible story about herself, built over twelve weeks, justified moving her salary, her seniority and her identity in one step.

Exhibit 1. The twelve weeks, from first application to offer
DateEvent
Monday 12 January 2026Starts applying cold through job portals
Monday 9 March 2026Week 8: after four screens and no offer, shifts to referrals and a bridge project
Monday 6 April 2026Week 12: final rounds complete
Wednesday 8 April 2026Written offer

Monday 12 January to Monday 6 April is exactly 12 weeks, 84 days. The pattern in those weeks, and what she changed, is the subject of this page.

2. The idea

Transitioning into product management means moving into a role whose daily work is deciding what to build and why, without the formal credential that role lacks everywhere. No degree licenses a product manager. India's market has no equivalent of a chartered accountancy. Hiring managers therefore substitute evidence: what you have already decided, with whom, and what happened. The pivot is a problem of evidence transfer: showing that judgment formed in another job already operates on product questions.

The problem the idea solves is asymmetric information. A hiring manager cannot observe a candidate's product judgment in a thirty-minute conversation, and a wrong hire costs months of a team's roadmap. The cheapest proxies are a previous product title, a famous employer, or a campus placement at an institution such as ISB or an IIM. A career-changer has none of these, so must manufacture a fourth: a visible track record of product decisions made inside the old role. Large product companies such as Flipkart and Razorpay, and the global capability centres (GCCs, India-based units of multinational firms) in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, have formalised the practice by running associate product manager programmes aimed at campus hires, but most transitions still happen lateral by lateral.

The sentence Harshita could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "I am not asking you to trust that engineers make good PMs; I am showing you three decisions I made about what not to build, and what each one cost or saved."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the middle three are the ones practitioners rarely say aloud.

First, name a specific target: not "product management" but, for Harshita, "a PM for payments or lending infrastructure where an engineering background shortens the learning curve". A named target lets the audit have a criterion. Second, audit. Every engineer, consultant or designer has made product decisions informally: which of five requests to build, which feature to cut when a deadline moved. The audit lists these, with the choice, the alternatives rejected, the evidence used and the outcome. Most candidates discover they have two or three real examples, not the twenty they feared having to invent.

Third, the bridge: a piece of work that sits visibly in the new role. Harshita asked Fulwari's own product lead for the right to write the discovery brief for a loan-reconciliation tool her team was already building. It took five weeks of evenings. Fourth, the route: a warm introduction converts far better than a cold application, for reasons shown below. Fifth, the story, which must be rehearsed until it takes ninety seconds and ends on the target company's problem, not on the candidate's ambition.

4. A worked example

Harshita kept a log. Her cold applications ran through portals between 12 January and 6 March (week 8); her referral-led applications, after the bridge brief existed, ran from 9 March to 6 April. Exhibit 2 shows the funnel. A screen is a first recruiter or manager call; a final is the last interview loop.

Exhibit 2. Applications to offers, by route
RouteApplicationsScreensScreen rateFinalsFinal rate (of screens)OffersOffer rate (of finals)
Cold portal8045.0%125.0%00.0%
Referral, after bridge20840.0%450.0%250.0%
Total / blended1001212.0%541.7%240.0%

Eighty applications gave four screens (4 / 80 = 5.0 per cent); twenty gave eight (8 / 20 = 40.0 per cent). Across both routes, 12 screens came from 100 applications, a blended 12.0 per cent, and 2 offers from 100 applications is 2.0 per cent. The blended figure hides the finding: the referral route produced a 10.0 per cent offer rate per application (2 / 20) against zero for the cold route. Both offers came from the route that carried a person and a piece of evidence.

Second pass. Suppose the referral screen rate had been 25 per cent, not 40, with everything else unchanged. Twenty applications give 5 screens, 2.5 finals at 50 per cent, and 1.25 expected offers (20 × 0.25 × 0.5 × 0.5), against the observed 2. The offer rate per referral application falls from 10.0 per cent to 6.25 per cent. A single input, the screen rate, accounts for the whole drop, and it is the input most sensitive to who vouches for you.

The pay arithmetic then decided the second question. Variable pay is a percentage of fixed pay; the equity grant of ₹16 lakh vests over four years, so counts as ₹4.00 lakh a year.

Exhibit 3. Annual package, in ₹ lakh
ComponentFulwari (current)Haveli offerHaveli, renegotiated
Fixed44.0036.0038.00
Variable (8% / 10% / 10% of fixed)3.523.603.80
Equity, annualised0.004.004.00
Total47.5243.6045.80
Shortfall against current—3.921.72
Shortfall as % of current—8.2%3.6%

Moving fixed pay by ₹2 lakh carries ₹0.20 lakh of extra variable pay with it, because variable is 10 per cent of fixed, so the gap closes by ₹2.20 lakh: from ₹3.92 lakh to ₹1.72 lakh, or from 8.2 per cent to 3.6 per cent of current pay. A transition priced this way is a bounded investment, not a leap.

5. Nuances a newcomer should know

Domain depth is an asset and a trap

Harshita understood loan reconciliation better than most PMs would. That earned her the screens. But engineers often answer product questions with architecture, and the interviewer hears an engineer who wants to build the thing, not decide whether to.

Title and role are different things

An "associate product manager" in a campus programme, a product manager at a thirty-person startup and a "product owner" who groomed a backlog at a services firm share nothing but vocabulary. Ask what decisions the role owns before comparing offers.

Each origin carries a different default

Consultants answer first and structure well, but under-invest in discovery with real users. Salespeople know one customer deeply and may generalise from the loudest account. Designers hold user empathy but often have not prioritised across competing demands. Analysts can measure but not frame the question. Exhibit 4 maps what each origin keeps and what it must unlearn.

Exhibit 4. What to keep and what to unlearn, by origin
OriginKeepUnlearn
EngineeringFeasibility judgment, credibility with the build teamAnswering with solutions; certainty about estimates
ConsultingStructuring, written synthesisRecommending without shipping; waiting for a complete answer
SalesCustomer proximity, objection handlingTreating one customer's request as the market
DesignUser empathy, critique of craftOwning the output rather than the trade-off
AnalyticsMetric design, scepticism about dataTreating measurement as a decision

The MBA route is a signalling device, not a substitute

A programme at ISB or an IIM gives campus access, an internship, and a cohort, which compress steps 3 and 4 of Figure 1. It does not remove the audit. Recruiters on campus still ask for a decision story.

A bridge must be verifiable

A side project nobody can inspect convinces nobody. A brief with a named reviewer, a shipped change, or a measured outcome can be checked, and checking is what the manager does.

Seniority resets, and you should plan for it

Many pivots reset level by one band. That is normal, not an insult; the question is whether the reset is recovered within two review cycles.

The story cannot tell you whether you will like the job

Product work is persuasion without authority. A well-built narrative proves you can pass an interview; it says nothing about whether you will enjoy a Tuesday of disagreement with four stakeholders. Shadow a PM for a week before leaving.

Questions before relying on a template story

Does my example show a decision or a task? Would the interviewer have chosen differently, and could I defend my choice? Is my target company's problem in the last sentence?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace, early and large

Exhibit 5. How the pivot differs by product type and company stage
ContextWhat the hiring manager weighs most
ConsumerTaste and experiment discipline; analysts and designers transition most easily
B2BCustomer-conversation depth and domain; engineers and sales people transition most easily
MarketplaceTwo-sided reasoning, supply and demand balance; operations and consulting backgrounds transfer well
Early-stageBreadth and speed; a founder or a generalist is credible without a bridge
Large or GCCProcess fluency and a visible internal sponsor; the internal move is often easier than the external one

The same candidate faces a different test in each cell. At a twenty-person start-up Harshita's bridge brief would count for less than her willingness to run support calls herself. At a GCC, a referral from an existing PM would matter more than the brief. The principle is constant: reduce the hiring manager's uncertainty at the cheapest cost to them.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 6. Mistakes, symptoms and diagnostics
MistakeSymptom seen from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Mass cold applyingMany applications, almost no screensVolume substitutes for evidenceCompute the screen rate after 30 applications; below 10% means change route
Credential chasingThree certificates, no decision storyCourses signal judgmentAsk: what did I decide that a course could not teach?
Narrating tasks"I wrote requirements and ran standups"Activity equals ownershipFor each story, name the alternative you rejected
Pitching ambitionStories end on "I want to grow into product"The interview is about the candidateRead the final sentence aloud; does it name their problem?

8. What good looks like

A well-run pivot looks unglamorous. By week 4 the candidate has a one-page audit with four decisions, each with alternatives and outcomes. By week 8 there is a bridge artifact with a named reviewer. Applications are fewer and routed through people: Harshita's twenty referral applications produced eight screens because each came with a three-line note and the brief attached. In interviews she opened with a decision, closed on Haveli's collections problem, and, when asked what she would cut, named a feature in the product. Gaurav later said the brief mattered less than the fact that she had defended a cut.

9. The decision

Harshita accepted Haveli's offer on Thursday 16 April 2026, one day before it lapsed, after renegotiating fixed pay from ₹36 lakh to ₹38 lakh. Her reasoning was the arithmetic, not optimism. A ₹1.72 lakh annual gap, 3.6 per cent of current pay, was affordable; the internal associate role offered no pay clarity and no external signal, and waiting a planning cycle risked the bridge going stale. She also asked for a six-month check-in on scope, recognising that a pivot is not complete at the offer.

To learn next: what a product manager does, since the role you are pivoting into defines what to unlearn, and then the career-switch narrative, which turns the audit in step 2 into the ninety-second story.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of your last five work decisions would survive the question "what did you choose not to do, and why?" Second, if your cold-application screen rate were 5 per cent, what is the cheapest person-shaped route you have not yet tried?
case20v1-craft.transition:
Disha Kulkarni and the Two Doors into Product

A decision case on transitioning into product management

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Disha Kulkarni sat in a corner of the third-floor cafeteria at Drishti Services in Pune, her laptop closed and two documents open on her phone. The first was an offer letter from Damru Exchange in Bengaluru for the role of Product Manager. It would lapse at close of business on Friday, 16 October, ten days away. The second was an email from Dipti Sethi, Drishti's head of product, confirming that Disha's application to move internally into an Associate Product Manager seat would go before the transfer committee on Wednesday, 14 October.

Disha was thirty-one and a senior engineer with eight years of experience, and she had wanted to become a product manager for three of them. Now two doors had opened in the same fortnight. She could not walk through both, and she suspected that choosing badly would cost her more than money.

2. Company background

Drishti Services, founded in 2011 in Pune, sells retail-analytics software to consumer-goods distributors and mid-sized chains. Its customers use it to forecast demand, track stock across warehouses and reconcile GST invoices with supplier claims. It has about 1,400 employees, engineering teams in Pune and Bengaluru, and revenue of roughly ₹620 crore. Its competitors include the in-house analytics teams of large retailers such as Reliance Retail and Tata's consumer businesses, as well as Zoho's inventory products and a long tail of niche vendors.

Damru Exchange is younger. Founded in 2019 in Bengaluru, it runs a business-to-business commerce network built on ONDC, connecting small manufacturers with institutional buyers. It has raised venture funding, employs about 300 people and is growing quickly.

3. The situation

Disha joined Drishti as an engineer and rose to lead the reconciliation engine, a service that matches supplier invoices against GST filings. Over three years she had begun sitting in on customer calls and rewriting the requirement documents her colleagues drafted.

In September she sat four mock product interviews, each scored out of five by a former product leader from Flipkart who volunteered to help. Exhibit 1 sets out the results. Disha scored well on technical depth and execution, as one would expect, but her average on product sense and on stakeholder influence was only 2.5 on a five-point scale, against 4.75 for technical depth. The reviewer wrote: "She solves the problem she is handed. A product manager's first job is to decide whether it is the right problem."

The two opportunities offered different compensation, shown in Exhibit 2. Drishti's internal APM seat sat in a lower band than her engineering level, so her year-one pay would fall. Damru's offer paid considerably more, including a one-time joining bonus. A third path, which her engineering director Dhruv Bhatia had pressed on her, was to stay and accept a promotion to Staff Engineer with formal ownership of the reconciliation roadmap.

Disha also asked colleagues abroad. Dagmar Weiss, a product designer in Amsterdam who had worked with her for two years, thought she had the instincts and told her, "Do not let anyone teach you that product management is project management with better slides."

4. The people

Dipti Sethi, head of product at Drishti in Pune, wants to build a bench of product managers who understand the platform deeply. She would sponsor Disha personally and put her under an experienced group product manager, but the APM band is fixed by policy and she cannot match Damru's pay.

Darshan Iyer, head of talent at Damru in Bengaluru, wants the offer accepted quickly. He needs the seat filled before the festival-season sales push and has hinted that the deadline could extend by three days, though not more.

Dhruv Bhatia, engineering director in Pune, wants Disha to stay in engineering. He regards her as the best engineer on his reconciliation team and fears the loss of a service she understands better than anyone. He believes the Staff Engineer path will hold her.

Dagmar Weiss, the designer in Amsterdam, has no stake in the outcome, and is the person Disha trusts most to say what she does not want to hear.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the most important of the three. It shows that her gap is not technical: her depth is near the ceiling. The weakness lies in judging which problem to solve and moving people who do not report to her. Exhibit 2 shows that the money pulls in the opposite direction from the skills gap. Path A costs her ₹5 lakh in the first year, while Path B pays ₹12 lakh more than she earns now, or ₹6 lakh more without the one-off bonus. Exhibit 3 shows the clock: the committee decides only two days before the Damru offer lapses.

6. The options

Option A: take the internal APM transfer. Disha would move on 1 November into Dipti's team under a named group product manager, running discovery on supplier reconciliation, a domain she knows better than anyone. The upside is a sponsor and a protected first year. The cost is a ₹5 lakh fall in year-one pay and a title, APM, that signals junior status to people who have only ever seen her as a senior engineer.

Option B: accept the Damru Exchange offer. She would serve her notice, leave Drishti on 15 December and join as a full Product Manager. The upside is the title, ₹58 lakh in year one and a growing business with real product decisions to make. The cost is that Damru would expect her to set priorities for a marketplace she has never used, with a new manager and no history of trust. The skills she lacks are exactly those a fast-moving firm tests first.

Option C: stay as Staff Engineer. She would accept Dhruv's promotion, own the reconciliation roadmap in an engineering capacity and revisit a product move in twelve to eighteen months. The upside is ₹51 lakh and comfortable standing. The cost is that the work that earned the promotion may reinforce the habits the reviewer criticised, and the APM seat may be filled by someone else.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which of Disha's existing strengths transfer directly into product management, and which habits from engineering will she need to unlearn?
  2. Which skills in Exhibit 1 can be built by studying and mock interviews, and which can only be built by doing the job? How does your answer change the value of a sponsor?
  3. Compare Options A and B using Exhibit 2. What would Disha need to believe about her first twelve months in each role for the pay difference to stop deciding the case?
  4. Which option would you choose, what would you ask Dipti or Darshan to change before you committed, and what would you do about the ten-day deadline in Exhibit 3?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a distinction that transitioning candidates often miss: the interview tests what you can say about product management, whereas the first year of the job tests what you can do. Engineers keep a great deal: precise thinking, credibility with the team that builds the product, and the ability to judge cost. What they usually have to unlearn is the instinct to treat a well-specified problem as a good one, to win arguments by being correct, and to measure progress by output shipped rather than outcome achieved.

A well-reasoned answer starts from Exhibit 1 rather than from Exhibit 2. Disha's gaps are in product sense and influence, which are learned by making decisions with consequences and watching how people react, and they are learned fastest under someone who corrects you early. That favours a setting with a sponsor over a setting with a larger cheque.

The defensible path is Option A, with two conditions negotiated before she accepts. First, a written review at nine months with a stated route to the full Product Manager band, so that the ₹5 lakh dip is bridged by a dated milestone and not by goodwill. Second, a named scope, such as supplier-claims discovery, that she owns end to end. The reasoning is that Option A attacks the weakness the scorecard identified, uses the domain knowledge that makes her unusual, and keeps the external market open: after twelve to eighteen months she could interview at Damru or its peers as a product manager with a shipped result and a credible reference. Option B offers more money, but it asks her to build the missing skills in public, without protection, while a new employer is judging her. Option C postpones the problem.

Option B is not indefensible, if she insisted on a clear first-ninety-day scope and an experienced manager. It cannot be defended on compensation alone.
case40v1-craft.transition:
Two Seats, Five Crafts

Madhura Apte and the slate at Mandara Lending Works — a case on transitioning into product management, from the selector's chair

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Madhura Apte had three documents open on the dining table of her flat in Thanisandra, in north Bengaluru, and no order she was willing to put them in. The first was a five-name interview scorecard. The second was a spreadsheet of compensation bands her own company had deliberately made narrower three years earlier. The third was a cure notice from Mangalam Finance Group's vendor-governance team, dated Friday, 30 October, saying in careful language that a product manager named in a contract schedule had not existed for sixty consecutive days and that Mandara Lending Works had thirty days to remedy that.

Apte was Vice-President, Product, at Mandara Lending Works, with two funded product-manager seats and five finalists for them. The hiring committee met at half past nine on Monday. By the end of it she was expected to say which two she wanted, at what level and on what terms — or that she wanted none of them, which was also an answer, and the one her chief executive would read as a failure of nerve.

What made the night long was not that the candidates were weak. It was that four of the five had produced almost the same score, by four entirely different routes, and that nobody in the building agreed on what the company's own history with such routes actually proved.

2. Mandara Lending Works, and the rung that was taken out

Mandara Lending Works was founded in Bengaluru in June 2016 by Mukund Rautela and two colleagues who had spent the previous decade building collections software for a private bank. Its product was unglamorous and sticky: a loan-origination and loan-management stack sold to non-banking financial companies, small finance banks and co-lending partnerships, which used it to score a borrower, disburse, and then chase repayment. By 2026 it had roughly 900 employees, engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, delivery pods in Nairobi and Warsaw, and annual revenue of about ₹410 crore.

The decision that shaped Apte's Monday had been taken in August 2023, and had nothing to do with hiring. A pay-parity review that year found Mandara's junior product titles were being used to pay women and internal transfers less for work indistinguishable from what full product managers did. The board's response was blunt and, most people still thought, correct: it abolished the Associate Product Manager level entirely. After August 2023 Mandara had exactly two product grades — Product Manager, with fixed pay from ₹36 lakh to ₹48 lakh, and Senior Product Manager, from ₹52 lakh to ₹68 lakh.

The consequence, three years on, was that Mandara had no landing step. Anyone switching into product from another craft arrived carrying a full product manager's scope, title and expectations from week one, in front of engineers and account directors who had known them in their previous life. There was no rung on which to be visibly learning.

3. The industry around the decision

Lending technology in India in 2026 was a regulated and crowded business. The Reserve Bank of India's digital-lending framework had pushed disclosure, grievance handling and first-loss-default-guarantee caps into the product itself; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made consent artefacts a shipping requirement rather than a legal annexe; the account-aggregator network had turned bank-statement analysis into a consent-and-latency problem. NPCI's UPI Autopay had quietly become the largest single determinant of collection efficiency for small-ticket lenders.

Competition came from three directions. Large financiers increasingly built in house, several with teams larger than Mandara's entire engineering group. Payment companies — Razorpay, Paytm and PhonePe among them — had merchant-lending arms with distribution Mandara could not match. And there was Maitri Credit Exchange, a Bengaluru rival four years younger, which had taken two of Mandara's co-lending accounts in 2025 by shipping a configurable waterfall for split disbursement nine months before Mandara managed it. Integrators such as Infosys and TCS bid the same deals as prime contractors.

Global exposure was real but lopsided. Twenty-two per cent of revenue came from outside India: a microfinance group served out of Nairobi, two consumer lenders in Poland handled from Warsaw, and an active prospect in Manila. The Warsaw clients produced the most demanding product requests and had, so far, no product manager in their time zone.

4. How the two seats came to be empty

Mandara's product function had grown by accident rather than design. In March 2022, facing a shortage of product managers who understood lending operations, Rautela approved a six-month Product Residency: six people from support, sales, design and engineering moved into product at their existing pay, each with a named mentor and a deliberately narrow scope. It was judged a success at the time and quietly discontinued in 2023, partly because the band restructure left nowhere to put a resident.

Between 2023 and the end of 2024, five more people switched into product from other crafts at Mandara, one at a time through ordinary internal postings; four of the five were given neither a mentor nor a narrowed scope. Eleven craft switchers in all. By June 2026 every one of the eleven had either completed eighteen months in the role or left before reaching it, which made the eighteen-month window comparable across the whole group. Five had left. Three were rated at or above the product manager bar.

Two things believed in 2024 had since turned out to be wrong. The first was that the residency had been expensive and the ad-hoc route cheap; when the people team finally cut the data by whether a mentor had been named, the pattern reversed so sharply that two senior people now cited the same eleven records to argue opposite cases. The second was that experienced external product managers ramped faster. Of three external hires since 2023, one was the strongest performer in the function and one had left inside a year, and with a sample of three nobody could say which was the pattern.

The immediate vacancy was ordinary. On Thursday, 2 July 2026, the product manager who owned the co-lending module resigned to join a payments company; she served sixty days and left on Monday, 31 August. A second seat, for collections, had been empty since a reorganisation in May. The requisition for both went out on Monday, 7 September. Ten weeks later Apte had the slate in Exhibit 1 and the scorecard in Exhibit 2.

5. The seven people in the room, and one who refused to be

Madhura Apte, 39, Vice-President, Product, Bengaluru. She had herself switched into product in 2017 from four years as a backend engineer, and knew the transition from the inside: the relief of no longer owning a pager, the shock of discovering that being right was not the same as being followed. Her stated position was that Mandara should prefer internal switchers who already understood lending operations, because domain ignorance had cost it the co-lending waterfall. What she was not saying was that her confidence rested on a sample of one — herself — and that the craft she could read fluently was the only craft absent from her slate.

Mukund Rautela, 48, co-founder and chief executive. His position was that the co-lending seat had to go to someone who had done the job before, because the Mangalam account was worth ₹34 crore a year and he had apologised for it once already. His incentive was a Series D conversation beginning in January. What he was not saying was that he had privately promised Mangalam's chief operating officer a named product manager by the end of November, in a call that appeared in no minutes.

Mihika Sardesai, 41, Director of Engineering, Pune, and the person who refused to be in the room. Two of her senior engineers had wanted to apply. She declined to release either, citing a re-architecture of the disbursement service running to March 2027, and did not attend the finalist loops. Her stated position was that product at Mandara did not need engineers, it needed people who could say no to sales. What she was not saying was that she had lost three engineers in eighteen months and regarded product as a leak.

Manav Chitale, 45, Chief Revenue Officer, Mumbai. He had put forward his best enterprise account director and attached a condition: the man must keep the Mangalam relationship for two quarters after moving. His incentive was a revenue number he would miss without that account. What he was not saying was that he expected a former account director in the product seat to be easier to push.

Mrinalini Barve, 37, Head of Talent, Bengaluru. She had built the eleven-person history in Exhibit 3 and read it as a caution: only three of the eleven craft switchers reached the bar, which was 27 per cent, and she would not sign another conversion without a funded programme behind it. Her incentive was a cost-per-hire target and an attrition number her own dashboard published. What she was not saying was that the recruiting sheet in Exhibit 4B and the finance office's note disagreed widely and that she had not reconciled them.

Malvika Thosar, 34, Group Product Manager, Bengaluru, the only person on the floor with a track record of growing a switcher. She read the same eleven records and reached the opposite conclusion: six of the seven switchers given a named mentor were still at Mandara, which was 86 per cent, and all four without a mentor were gone. She wanted the strongest person she could get. What she was not saying was that she had capacity to mentor one person properly, not two, and had already told her partner she would look outside in the new year.

Marta Zabel, 36, Delivery Lead, Warsaw. Her position was that the second seat belonged in Europe, where the hardest requirements originated and where she was writing specifications at night. A product manager hired in Warsaw would cost about ₹95 lakh a year fully loaded, most of the budget for both Indian seats. What she was not saying was that she wanted the role herself.

Mwangi Githaiga, 43, Delivery Lead, Nairobi. He had asked for nothing, which Apte found more unsettling than a demand. His one written comment was that the microfinance client's collections requirements had waited fourteen months and that he no longer raised them.

The five finalists

Mandar Phadnis, 34, enterprise account director, Mumbai, nine years in sales. Internal. He knew the Mangalam contract better than Apte did and could read a lender's operating model in an hour. Twice in his loop he answered a prioritisation question by describing what the customer had asked for.

Mallika Soman, 31, senior product designer, Bengaluru, six years. Internal. She had run the collections-app research behind Mandara's only genuinely original feature in two years. She had never owned a number, and called roadmap trade-offs “mostly a question of being honest with people.”

Murtuza Contractor, 32, implementation lead, Bengaluru, four and a half years — three of them at Mahanadi Advisory Partners before joining Mandara eighteen months ago. Internal. The most structured thinker in the slate and the most comfortable with data. His weakness, two interviewers said independently, was producing frameworks where a decision was wanted.

Mayur Panse, 36, external. Co-founder of Machaan Retail Collective, a kirana-commerce venture that wound down in March 2026 after four years; he drew ₹15 lakh in its final year. He had built, priced, sold and shut a product. He had never had a manager, and scored lowest of the five on influence without authority — a result one interviewer called “an artefact of asking a founder to describe persuading people who outrank him.”

Mitali Saraiya, 33, external, currently a product manager at Maitri Credit Exchange, with four years in the role. She shipped the split-disbursement waterfall that cost Mandara two accounts. She wanted ₹52 lakh fixed, above the top of Mandara's product manager band, and had ninety days' notice.

6. Exhibits

A disagreement the case does not resolve. Mrinalini Barve and Malvika Thosar are both reading Exhibit 3, and both are arithmetically right. Barve's figure is 3 of 11 reaching the bar, or 27 per cent. Thosar's is 6 of the 7 mentored switchers still in place, or 86 per cent. Nobody at Mandara has reconciled the two readings, and neither has been shown to be the better guide. Exhibit 4B carries a second, separate disagreement, between the recruiting team's sheet and the finance office's note, which is also unreconciled.

7. Voices

“I do not need a product manager who will learn lending. I need a product manager who will not lose me the second account in two years. If that costs an exception to a band, write the exception.”

— Mukund Rautela, leadership review, 4 November 2026

“Three out of eleven reached the bar. If an engineering manager brought me a process with that yield I would shut it down, not scale it.”

— Mrinalini Barve, finalist debrief, 9 November 2026

“You are reading the denominator you prefer. Six of the seven we actually invested in are still here. All four of the ones we threw into the deep end are gone. The eleven is not one programme, it is two, and only one of them is ours.”

— Malvika Thosar, replying in the same debrief

“Keep Mandar on Mangalam till March and I will support the move in writing. Take him off it and I will say in the QBR that product took my account director in the middle of a renewal.”

— Manav Chitale, message to Apte, 11 November 2026

“Please note I am not applying. I am saying that whoever you hire in Bengaluru will be asleep when Warsaw is deciding. We have shipped two releases this quarter that nobody in product read before they went out.”

— Marta Zabel, email, 12 November 2026

“In the loop I was asked how I would get a team to adopt a decision they disagreed with. At Machaan I just decided. I have been honest that I do not know how to do it the other way yet.”

— Mayur Panse, follow-up call with Apte, 13 November 2026

“Schedule 4 says ‘a dedicated product manager’. It does not define the term and we have never asked them what they would accept. I would not assume the answer is a person with that exact designation, and I would not assume it is not.”

— Note from Mandara's contracts counsel, 13 November 2026

8. The options as Apte has framed them

Option 1 — two internal transfers: Phadnis and Soman. Year-one cost ₹91 lakh, nine lakh inside budget, and a visible signal that Mandara promotes from within. Both start on 15 January after a forty-five-day handover, well after the cure notice expires. Chitale's condition makes Phadnis half a product manager until March, neither has owned a roadmap, and Thosar can mentor only one of them properly.

Option 2 — Contractor internally and Saraiya from Maitri. Year-one cost ₹99 lakh, inside budget by a single lakh, and a proven product manager on co-lending. But Saraiya's ninety-day notice means she cannot start before the first week of March 2027, and her ₹52 lakh fixed requires the exception the band change was designed to prevent. The two people most likely to resent that exception, Soman and Contractor, are on the same slate.

Option 3 — Panse on co-lending now, Soman on collections. Year-one cost ₹94 lakh. Panse is the only finalist who can be in the seat before the cure notice expires. He scored highest on product sense and lowest on influence, has never reported to anyone, and would be setting priorities for a regulated module he has never built.

Option 4 — fill one seat now and reopen the residency for the second. A six-month mentored placement at existing pay with narrowed scope, which is what panel A of Exhibit 3 suggests actually worked. It needs board approval, because after August 2023 there is no grade to put a resident in, and the board would read it as reinstating the rung it removed for reasons of fairness that have not gone away.

Each of the four assumes the problem is which people to select. None tests whether the co-lending seat needs a product manager at all rather than a technical programme manager carrying the designation the contract schedule names; none asks whether the collections seat should be in Bengaluru, Warsaw or Nairobi; none asks what Mandara would have to change about the job so that a switcher could survive its first six months. Panel A of Exhibit 3 can be read as saying the failure rate is a property of the onboarding rather than of the candidates, in which case the slate is the wrong object of attention altogether.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee sits at 9.30 on Monday, 16 November. The cure notice expires on Sunday, 29 November; counsel thinks Mangalam unlikely to invoke the ₹25 lakh quarterly service credit if it can see a signed offer, but “unlikely” is doing a great deal of work in that sentence. The two seats carry a combined year-one compensation budget of ₹1 crore, set in the September plan and not reopened; any pair in Exhibit 4A above ₹100 lakh sends Rautela back to the board in the middle of a funding conversation. Internal moves require a forty-five-day handover under Mandara's own policy. Saraiya's notice is ninety days and Maitri has historically enforced it. Phadnis's ₹11 lakh incentive protection sits outside the seat budget and is unapproved. Thosar has capacity for one mentee. And Sardesai will not release an engineer before March 2027, so whatever Apte decides, the one route into product she personally understands is closed this year.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. For each finalist, name the two things their prior craft gives them and the one habit from it most likely to make them a poor product manager in the first six months. Where does Exhibit 2 help, and where does it mislead?
  2. Exhibit 2 gives four of the five the same average of 3.6. What would you change — the dimensions, the weights, the rounding, or the panel — so that it discriminates between a designer, a salesperson, a consultant and a founder rather than averaging their differences away?
  3. Barve reads Exhibit 3 as 27 per cent and Thosar reads it as 86 per cent, and both are correct. Which denominator should the committee use on Monday, and what further data would settle it — or can data not settle it?
  4. Exhibit 4B makes an internal transfer both the cheapest and the dearest option, depending on whose sheet you read. Which assumption in the finance note would you attack first, and how would the answer change what you offer Phadnis, Soman and Contractor?
  5. The band change of August 2023 was made for reasons of fairness that still hold. Can Mandara create a landing step for craft switchers without recreating the abuse the board abolished? Design the mechanism, and say what it costs.
  6. It is 9.30 on Monday, 16 November. What does Apte propose, in one sentence, and which constraint does she break to do it? If Rautela takes her to the board in January, what does she say when a director asks why the product function cannot reliably convert its own people — and what would she have had to measure, starting Monday, to answer differently next year?

It was past one when Apte stopped. She had written one line at the top of a fresh page — what would make a switcher succeed here? — and nothing under it. The scorecard said four of them were the same person. The eleven records said whatever the reader needed them to say. The contract said thirty days, of which fourteen remained. She turned off the lamp without deciding, which was itself a decision she had nine hours to reverse.
exp20v2-craft.first.90:
Your first 90 days in a PM role

Learn the product, the people and the numbers before changing anything.

1. The pack on the first morning

On Monday 6 April 2026, Ishani Khanvilkar arrived at the Pune office of Hundi Settlement Exchange, a business-to-business service that moves money from buyers to distributors' bank accounts. Each movement is a settlement instruction: a request to the banks to credit a merchant. Hundi served 5,000 merchants and handled 12,50,000 instructions a month, worth ₹1,500 crore, an average of ₹12,000 each. Settlements were new to Ishani.

Her manager, Hemant Kirpalani, head of product, handed her a first-day pack with three items: a roadmap, a dashboard screenshot reading "settlement success 97.6%", and a commitment. The board had been promised a retry engine, an automatic resender for failed instructions costing ₹1.80 crore, by Tuesday 30 June. Her predecessor, Jatin Kothari, had moved to the lending team. "You have fresh eyes," Hemant said. "Tell me what is broken."

The pressure ran in two directions. If she changed things in week two she would be altering a system she could not yet describe, and her team of 14 would be following a plan written by someone ignorant of their history. If she produced nothing, 30 June would arrive and the retry engine would ship by default, justified by a number nobody had checked. Her review with Hemant was fixed for Friday 3 July, three days after that deadline and day 89 of her tenure.

2. The idea

A transition is the period in which a person takes over a role and is still a net cost to the organisation: others spend time teaching them, correcting them and waiting for them. The first-90-days discipline says that this period should be sequenced, not improvised: learn first, diagnose second, change third, in that order, with the order enforced by calendar rather than mood. Michael Watkins, then a Harvard Business School professor, set the approach out in The First 90 Days (2003), drawing on studies of executives who stumbled after promotion. His organising measure was the breakeven point: the day on which the newcomer has contributed as much value as they have consumed.

For a product manager the problem is sharper than for most. A PM has no authority to compel anyone, so the only currency is credibility, and credibility is spent fastest by confident statements that turn out to be wrong. The discipline ensures the first confident statement is made on day 60, after checking, rather than on day 6, after hearing.

The sentence Ishani could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib: "For the first ninety days I am buying information, and I will spend it on change only once I can say what each number means, who owns it, and what the team has already tried."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have seven steps, several of which are usually left unspoken. First, map the system: follow one real instruction from a merchant's invoice to the credit in their account, noting every handoff. Second, run a fixed listening protocol. Ishani held 35 conversations in the first 30 days: eight with engineers, six with customer-operations staff, ten with merchants, four with sales, three with finance and four with others. They totalled 1,410 minutes, or 23.5 hours. Every one used the same five questions, including "what have you already tried?" and "what should I not touch?", so that answers could be compared.

Third, keep a claims ledger: a running list of every factual assertion she heard, with its source and a status. Fourth, verify the claims that carry weight by re-deriving them from raw records. Fifth, sort promises from preferences: the retry engine was a promise to the board, whereas Jatin's preference for a particular queueing design was merely a habit. Sixth, take one deliberately small action by about day 45 to show she acts: she fixed a misleading label on the merchant statement. Seventh, hold a diagnosis readout on day 60, Thursday 4 June, and a plan on day 90.

The ledger is the step most newcomers skip, and it is the one that exposes the hidden quality of inherited knowledge. Table 1 shows Ishani's by 4 June.

Table 1. Claims ledger, 6 April to 4 June 2026
SourceClaims loggedVerifiedHeld upWrong or incomplete
Head of product5321
Engineering7541
Customer operations6431
Sales4211
Finance2211
Total2416115

Of 24 claims, she verified 16 (66.7 per cent). Of those 16, 11 held up (68.75 per cent) and five were wrong or incomplete. Every source, including her own manager, contributed at least one claim that failed. Nobody was lying; each repeated what had once been true or was true under a narrower definition. Treat every inherited claim as a hypothesis with a source.

4. A worked example: what does 97.6 per cent mean?

The dashboard's headline was the first claim Ishani chose to re-derive. She asked Jyoti Kamat, the analyst, for the raw instruction log for March: 12,50,000 rows. The dashboard counted an instruction as a success when the bank accepted it, which happened for 12,20,000 rows. Arithmetic: 12,20,000 divided by 12,50,000 is 0.976, or 97.6 per cent. The dashboard was correct. It answered a question no merchant asks.

A merchant asks whether the money arrived today. Credit on the same working day is called T+0 ("transaction day plus zero"). Only 11,25,000 instructions met that test: 11,25,000 divided by 12,50,000 is 90.0 per cent. The gap, 12,20,000 minus 11,25,000, is 95,000 instructions, or 7.6 percentage points. Table 2 breaks the whole month into mutually exclusive outcomes, valued at ₹12,000 each.

Table 2. March 2026 instructions by outcome (value = instructions x ₹12,000)
OutcomeInstructionsShare (%)Value (₹ crore)
Credited same day (T+0)11,25,00090.001,350.0
Accepted, sent after the bank's daily cut-off76,0006.0891.2
Accepted, delayed for other reasons19,0001.5222.8
Rejected or failed30,0002.4036.0
Total12,50,000100.001,500.0

A cut-off is the time each day after which a bank treats an instruction as belonging to the next working day. The retry engine would address only the 30,000 failures: ₹36 crore of monthly value. Late submission, 76,000 instructions worth ₹91.2 crore, was two and a half times larger and untouched by the roadmap.

Now the second pass, changing one input: the definition of success. Table 3 holds the data constant and varies only the test.

Table 3. One month, three definitions of "success"
DefinitionCountedRate (%)Not countedValue not counted (₹ crore)
Accepted by bank12,20,00097.6030,00036.0
Credited same day (T+0)11,25,00090.001,25,000150.0

The T+1 count is 11,25,000 plus all 76,000 late-cut-off instructions plus 7,000 of the 19,000 others, which is 12,08,000. The remaining 12,000 of those 19,000, with the 30,000 failures, give the 42,000 uncounted. Change the definition and the "success rate" moves across 7.6 points with no change in the underlying system. The first lesson of the ninety days is that a number is a question plus a data set, and Ishani had been handed only the answer.

5. Nuances a newcomer must learn

Listening is work with a deliverable

Ishani sent Hemant a one-page note every Friday: what she had learned, what she doubted, what she would do next. Learning that cannot be seen cannot be credited or corrected.

A metric is not its definition

The dashboard figure and the thing it was meant to proxy had drifted apart. Always ask for the definition, the denominator and the date it was last changed before using any inherited number.

Promises differ from preferences

The retry engine was a commitment to the board; the queueing design was a taste. Renegotiate promises openly; drop preferences without ceremony.

Inheritances differ in kind

Watkins distinguished start-ups, turnarounds, realignments and sustaining-success situations. A product in crisis needs faster diagnosis than one that is healthy; the three-phase calendar is a default, not a law.

Waiting excludes emergencies

The rule forbids discretionary change. If settlements stop reaching merchants on a Tuesday, a newcomer acts at once and says so. Declare the exception to your manager the moment you use it.

It cannot tell you whether the strategy is right

Ninety days of listening reveals the system's present state and its history. It does not reveal whether settlements are a good business to be in, or what competitors will do next. Those need separate work.

Ask before you rely

Who benefits if this number looks good? When was it last audited? What would the team do if it were false?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; small and large firms

The method is constant; the source of truth shifts. Table 4 summarises where the first month goes in each type of product.

Table 4. Where the learning comes from
Product typeRichest sourceTypical trap
ConsumerEvent data and support tickets across millions of usersAverages hiding segments with opposite behaviour
B2BA handful of named accounts and their contractsSales promises never written into the roadmap
MarketplaceSupply and demand sides measured separatelyFixing one side and starving the other

Hundi is B2B, so Ishani's ten merchant conversations outweighed any dashboard. A consumer PM with crores of users cannot meet a representative sample, so the first month leans on data, and the danger is trusting event definitions nobody has read. In a marketplace, the newcomer must learn both customer groups and the balance between them before touching either.

Size changes the shape. At an early-stage company, with perhaps 15 people, the three phases compress and overlap: the newcomer may be expected to ship something in week three, and a fast, small, reversible change is acceptable if the diagnosis is honest about how thin it is. At a large company the stakeholders multiply, governance cycles are quarterly, and day 90 may fall before the next planning round, so the unwritten work is mapping who must agree to anything.

7. Common mistakes

Arriving with a plan

Symptom: a roadmap deck circulates by week three. Misunderstanding: seniority entitles a view before evidence. Cheapest diagnostic: ask yourself what observation would change the plan; if none, it is a belief, not a plan.

Trusting the dashboard

Symptom: a headline figure is quoted without its definition. Misunderstanding: a number that is displayed has been checked. Diagnostic: re-derive one figure from raw records; it takes an afternoon, and Ishani's took one.

Listening only inwards

Symptom: no external customer conversation by day 30. Misunderstanding: colleagues know what customers think. Diagnostic: count external conversations; target at least a quarter of the total, and Ishani's ten were 10 of 35.

Learning invisibly

Symptom: the manager asks in week five what you have been doing. Misunderstanding: output is the only evidence of work. Diagnostic: could your manager state your three best insights today? If not, write them down this week.

8. What good looks like

By Thursday 4 June a well-run transition leaves a reader with four things. A one-page map of the system. A ledger showing which claims held. A re-derived headline number, with its definition stated. And a short list of open questions the newcomer admits she cannot yet answer. Ishani's readout had exactly these. Hemant did not agree with all of it, but he could see which statements were evidence and which judgement. She presented his 97.6 per cent as a finding about the dashboard's definition, not about anyone's competence.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 4 June Ishani proposed to Hemant that the ₹1.80 crore retry engine be deferred and that the 30 June commitment be redefined as a cut-off-aware scheduler, costing ₹0.40 crore, piloted on 1,000 merchants (20 per cent of the base). Her reasoning ran from Table 2: the scheduler targeted 76,000 instructions, 2.5 times the failures the retry engine could touch. If scheduling alone rescued half of them, 38,000, same-day credit would rise to 11,63,000 of 12,50,000, or 93.04 per cent. She flagged what she did not know: how many late submissions were within merchants' control. Hemant agreed to take the revised commitment to the board.

Her next step is a transition of a different kind: the summer internship and its conversion to an offer, which compresses the same sequence into about ten weeks and makes visible learning the whole case for conversion. Inheriting an existing product is the natural companion topic.

Two questions to sit with. First, which number do you currently quote with confidence that you have never re-derived, and what would it cost to do so this week? Second, if your manager had to choose between your plan and your ledger, which would show more of your judgement?
exp40v2-craft.first.90:
Your first 90 days in a PM role

Learn the product, the people and the numbers before changing anything — and know when that rule stops being true.

1. Two arrivals, two inherited commitments

On Monday 5 January 2026, Sharvari Udeshi joined Tarazu Pricing Systems in Pune as senior product manager for its core product: price and margin software for pharmaceutical and packaged-goods distributors, working inside the ceilings the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority fixes. The business was 42 enterprise accounts and ₹46.20 crore of annual recurring revenue, averaging ₹1.10 crore an account.

Shantanu Dharap, vice-president of product, gave her three things: a tile reading Adoption 78.6%; a commitment her predecessor Sanket Vichare had made to two large customers and then the board, that Tarazu Copilot, a natural-language price-query assistant, would be live by Tuesday 31 March 2026 at a cost of ₹2.40 crore; and a renewal calendar on which eleven of the 42 accounts, carrying ₹11.40 crore, renewed by 30 June. Her ninetieth day, Saturday 4 April, fell on a weekend, so the plan review was set for Thursday 2 April, day 88. The Copilot deadline was day 86.

A week later, on Monday 12 January, Tushar Saranjame joined Sawaari Auto Exchange in Bengaluru as product manager for the supply side. Sawaari is a used two-wheeler marketplace in nine cities: sellers list, Sawaari inspects and certifies, buyers browse only certified stock. In December 2025 sellers created 1,84,000 listings, 32,200 were certified, and 11,270 vehicles sold at an average ₹46,500. At 4.2 per cent commission — ₹1,953 a sale — that was ₹52.41 crore of gross merchandise value and ₹2.20 crore of revenue. Urvashi Natekar, his manager, repeated the settled view that afternoon: Sawaari had a demand problem. The dated commitment was a price-guidance engine for sellers at ₹1.15 crore, due Wednesday 15 April 2026 — day 94, four days past his ninetieth day of Saturday 11 April.

Both inherited a headline number, a diagnosis and a dated promise. Neither had standing on day one to challenge any of the three, and in both cases silence would ship the promise.

2. The idea, and the four schools that read it differently

A transition is the interval in which someone new to a role consumes more organisational value than they produce: colleagues teach, correct and wait. The discipline holds that it should be sequenced — learn, diagnose, change — with the order enforced by a calendar rather than appetite, and a dated readout at each seam.

The lineage is older than the phrase. John Gabarro of Harvard Business School, in The Dynamics of Taking Charge (1987), found that taking charge ran through stages, took longer than expected, and that the newcomers who failed acted on a diagnosis imported from their last job. Michael Watkins compressed the prescription into The First 90 Days (2003) and supplied its measure, the breakeven point: the day cumulative contribution equals cumulative consumption. Your Next Move (2009) added the STARS taxonomy — start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment, sustaining success.

Four positions can be signed or refused. The sequenced-learning school — Gabarro through Watkins to Marty Cagan's instruction that a new PM spend one to three months becoming expert on the users, the data and the business — will sign: no discretionary change before the newcomer can re-derive the headline number from raw records. It will not sign a fixed thirty-day wait regardless of situation type; STARS denies that.

The early-delivery school, strongest in fast-growing companies, will sign: ship one visible, reversible improvement within three weeks, because credibility is bought with shipped work, not interviews. It will not sign reordering the roadmap in week three; shipping small and rewriting the plan are different acts.

The mandate-negotiation school treats the transition as contracting and will sign: most failed transitions are mandate failures, not learning failures — newcomer and manager never agreed in writing on situation type, success, resources and review date. It will not sign that more listening would have saved them.

The selection school, loudest among career practitioners, will sign: the outcome is largely set before day one, by what the candidate verified during selection. It will not sign that a well-run ninety days can repair a mis-sold role.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the steps left implicit

The newcomer walks one unit of work end to end: Sharvari followed one price revision from a distributor's commercial team to the chemist's invoice. The listening is protocolised, the same questions put to everyone so answers compare, with external voices quotaed: Tushar's thirty-one first-month conversations included fourteen sellers and four buyers. Inherited assertions go into a claims ledger as hypotheses with sources, rather than being absorbed as facts. The readout is dated before any of it begins, which stops learning filling ninety days.

Three implicit steps carry the value. Learn the cadence rather than the system: budget rounds, renewal dates, filings and lead times decide which choices exist on day 90. Know what the small early action is for — demonstration, not impact, so choose for reversibility and witness count. Separate promises from preferences: a promise to a customer is renegotiated in the open, a predecessor's taste simply dropped, and a newcomer who confuses the two apologises for architecture and quietly breaks commitments.

Her quantitative work began with the tile. Tarazu counted an account as adopted if any user had logged in within ninety days; 33 of 42 had, and 33 divided by 42 is 78.6 per cent. The figure was correct: it measured breadth of login. The product's value came from price changes published through Tarazu rather than keyed into the distributor's ERP afterwards, so she asked Tanaya Belvalkar, the revenue analyst, to band every account by the share of changes going through the product. Seventeen of 42 published more than half of theirs through Tarazu: 40.5 per cent. Two defensible numbers, 38.1 percentage points apart, on one month and one customer base.

Table 1. Tarazu Pricing Systems: the 42-account base at 31 December 2025, by depth of use, with eight quarters of renewal history

Deep (above 75%)914.401.60213 / 1492.9
