Read that column as its reciprocal and the spread is stark: Kinara costs 26.7 hours per expected offer, Dhaatri 28.6, Gopuram 40.9, Girvi 93.3. Girvi's brief is longest and its conversion weakest — a firm compensating for an undisciplined later loop.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. At senior levels, where the job is organisational navigation, a document written alone measures the wrong construct. In thin markets — Girija's own, where perhaps forty people in India combine consumer scale with lending exposure — it removes more good candidates than bad. And where the difficulty is operating inside constraint, a sanitised brief strips out the friction.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

Two-sided products break single-objective briefs. Kinara's first draft asked for better shipper conversion, which anyone competent can get by subsidising supply; the rubric had no line for truck-owner economics. Expert practice puts both sides in tension and the trade-off in the rubric.

Regulated products invert the relationship between realism and fairness. Girvi operates under lending rules it cannot describe in a brief, so the brief either omits the binding constraint, making the exercise fiction, or includes enough that only insiders can answer, turning a skills test into a credential test. Mature firms resolve this with a two-page constraints annexe.

Hardware compounds the problem with time. Dhaatri Medtech Industries builds connected diagnostic devices hostage to tooling lead times of six to nine months, which no three-hour exercise conveys. Dhaatri's answer was honest: a one-page sequencing memo, with the hard content moved into a live session with a hardware engineer.

AI-native products mean the instrument now measures a mixture. Kautuk Reasoning Labs, twenty-two people building retrieval tooling, found assisted drafting had compressed the visible quality distribution: submissions uniformly well-structured, uniformly thin on the choices that mattered. At the organisational seam, recruiting owns candidate experience, hiring managers own the rubric, nobody owns validity, so the brief drifts — a line added each round, none removed. Firms claim annual rubric reviews; mostly they rewrite when a hiring manager leaves.

6. Eight distinctions between the expert and the competent

A take-home is a gate, not a ranking, unless you have shown otherwise.

Competent teams rank by score and interview the top decile. The expert asks what separates the eighteenth candidate from the nineteenth and, finding it is 1.4 points on a scale with a 6.625-point reviewer gap, uses the score only to exclude the unprepared. The tell is a debrief where someone says "she scored 74, he scored 71" as though that gap exists.

The obvious reading of a low return rate is wrong.

Ninety of 240 did not return Kinara's brief, and the comfortable reading is that the filter removed the uncommitted. The expert reading is that non-return tracks employment and caring responsibilities, both of which rise with seniority. The tell is a non-return rate higher among experienced candidates — what the callbacks showed.

Agreement on averages is not agreement.

Kaushik and Damayanti differed by 1.625 points on the mean and 6.625 per document. An expert never accepts mean severity as calibration evidence; she asks for the distribution of absolute gaps, because symmetric noise has mean zero by construction.

Polish is now free, so polish is now noise.

Before 2023 a well-structured document was weak evidence of structured thinking. It no longer is. The response is not to ban assistance but to shift weight onto what tools do badly: choosing between two defensible options, and saying what would make you abandon your plan. The tell is a rubric where clarity still carries twenty points.

The defence round is the validity check, not a formality.

Twenty-five minutes asking why the second release sits behind the first, and what was cut, recovers most of the signal the page withholds. The expert scores it on the same rubric. The tell that a company has missed this is a defence round run by someone who has not read the submission.

Length is a design variable with a known cost curve.

Kinara's four stated hours became 7.5 real ones, an overrun of 1.875 times; Table 4's budgets imply 34 over 19, or 1.79. Experts plan for roughly double and write hard artefact limits — three pages, two exhibits — because a page limit binds and a time budget does not.

The instrument must be validated against outcomes, and almost never is.

The expert's first question of any established take-home is the correlation between score and nine-month rating. Usually nobody has looked. Section 8 shows what happens when someone does.

What the candidate ignores is the richest signal on the page.

A brief should contain one irrelevant constraint and one load-bearing one. Competent reviewers score completeness; experts score what the candidate declined and whether she said why. The tell is a submission addressing every bullet equally — compliance, not judgement.

7. By product type and company stage

Consumer briefs can be written honestly in three hours because the product is inspectable. Granth Learning Works asks candidates to improve week-four retention for a cohort of its own users, funnel numbers supplied. Enterprise briefs cannot be inspected and must supply context: good ones carry two pages of annexe, bad ones ask candidates to guess the buyer. A B2B brief must name a buyer who is not the user: one about freight-booking software that never mentions the logistics head who signs is not a B2B brief. Marketplace briefs need the two-sided tension above; hardware briefs a stated lead time; AI briefs a stated error rate and a question about what happens when the model is wrong.

Stage changes the economics, not the principles. A twenty-two-person company cannot amortise 200 reviewer hours across nine hires, and should not pretend to a rubric it will apply twice; its honest instrument is a short paid trial. A firm hiring nine PMs a year has volume for anchored rubrics and a validation study, and its failure is the opposite: a process so standardised it hires people good at the process. Asserted but not real: that enterprise candidates tolerate longer briefs.

8. Three rounds with numbers, one a failure

First, Kinara's redesign, which worked. Dhanashree cut the brief to a ninety-minute exercise with a three-page limit, published the six rubric headings and weights, kept two blind reviewers and added a twenty-five-minute defence. The round opening on Monday 11 January 2027, thirteen weeks after her 12 October recommendation, sent the same 240 briefs.

The 67 per cent is 133.8 falling to 43.9; the 15 per cent is ₹9,00,000 falling to ₹7,65,000. What did not improve is reliability: Dhanashree did not re-run the noise audit, so she cannot say whether the shorter brief measures the same thing more cheaply, or something different.

Second, Girvi Lending Exchange, where the instrument failed outright. Its eight-hour brief asked candidates to design a collections product for borrowers in arrears. Eighteen PMs were hired across eight rounds between January 2024 and December 2025, and in early 2026 a new head of product compared their scores with their nine-month ratings.

The brief violated claim one: no Girvi PM designs a collections product alone, because regulation puts legal and risk in the room from week one. The exercise measured willingness to write confidently about the unknowable. The recovery was not abolition: Girvi substituted a two-hour exercise on a shipped feature plus a forty-five-minute walkthrough with a risk officer, and committed to re-validating.

Third, Kautuk Reasoning Labs, which bought its way out. It paid eleven candidates ₹15,000 each for a six-hour project — ₹2,500 an hour, ₹1,65,000 in total — and got four offers and three joiners. The headline ₹55,000 per join flattered the scheme by ignoring founder time: four reviewer hours per trial, forty-four in all, at a loaded ₹5,200 an hour, or ₹2,28,800. True cost ₹3,93,800 across three joiners is ₹1,31,267 per join — above Kinara's round-one ₹1,00,000. The paid trial is not cheaper; it is more expensive, more predictive and fairer, and the honest argument says so.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The brief becomes unpaid consultancy. Early sign: the output is useful to the company. Diagnostic: would we act on this if a candidate wrote it well? If yes, shrink it or pay. Caught late, the cost is reputational.

Scores drift toward presentation. Early sign: top scorers share a formatting idiom. Diagnostic: re-score ten submissions stripped to plain text. Caught late, two years of hires share one blind spot.

Reviewers are never calibrated. Early sign: a mean absolute gap above five points, as at Kinara. Diagnostic: score three documents jointly before the round opens, discussing every gap above four. Caught late, the cost is invisible: nobody tracks the candidates a coin flip rejected.

Nobody validates. Early sign: "it has worked well for us". Diagnostic: the Table 6 exercise. Caught late, the instrument has been wrong for eight rounds and every hire rationalised individually.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Abolish the unpaid take-home. The strongest form rests on the 2022 re-ranking: if structured interviews predict at 0.42 and work samples at 0.33, the higher-validity instrument also costs candidates nothing, and Table 1's 1,204 hours are a deadweight transfer. It would be wrong if the two measure different constructs and combine, making incremental validity substantial. That study, for product management, does not exist.

Keep it, and pay. The strongest form concedes everything about unpaid labour and answers with money, as Kautuk did. It rests on Spence: a costly signal is informative, and payment removes the confound with free time. It would be wrong if payment reintroduces bias by changing who participates — plausible in India, where ₹15,000 is a real incentive at some income levels and a rounding error at others.

Keep it unpaid, make it small, treat it as a gate. The strongest form is managerial, not psychometric: ninety minutes costs the market little, removes candidates who cannot write a coherent page, and does not pretend to rank. Dhanashree's round two is this position. It would be wrong if ninety minutes has reliability so low that even the gate is arbitrary — what her unrepeated audit would have answered. No synthesis commands assent; the method does: measure reliability, estimate candidate hours, validate, then argue.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a better brief. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. She can state her instrument's reliability and when it was measured. She knows her candidate-hours-per-hire figure and treats it as a cost she owns, not an externality. She will drop a criterion she cannot anchor in an observable behaviour, even one she believes in. And from the candidate's chair she reads a brief as information: a nine-hour unscored exercise says more about how a firm will treat her time than its hiring manager will.

12. What each of them decided

Dhanashree Kalgutkar recommended on 12 October 2026 that the written exercise survive in reduced form. Her reasoning was not that it predicted well — she could not show that — but that Table 1 exposed a cost of 133.8 candidate hours per hire she could cut by two-thirds without losing the only stage producing a reviewable artefact. She also committed to repeating the noise audit each round, and to a validation study at eighteen hires.

Girija Deolekar did the arithmetic in Table 4 and sent real work to Kinara and Dhaatri, eleven hours of the thirty-four the table totals, for a 36 per cent chance of at least one offer. Spreading her hours across all four would not buy the 58 per cent Table 4 gives at full effort, because full effort needs all thirty-four hours. Fourteen is 41 per cent of that depth, at which her pass probabilities fall by about two-thirds: offer probabilities of 0.077, 0.061, 0.053 and 0.079, and a 24 per cent chance of at least one offer. She withdrew from Girvi in a courteous email saying the eight-hour brief was more than she could do justice to, and told Gopuram she would answer in three weeks if the role stayed open. Two of the four could have learned something true from her reply. Neither asked.

Three questions. If Dhanashree's shorter brief has a single-rater reliability of 0.40 rather than 0.62, is her gate still defensible, and how would she find out? Girija's withdrawal is individually rational and collectively corrosive, since those who can afford to refuse are the ones a company most wants — what breaks that equilibrium? And if incremental validity over a structured interview is near zero, what are Table 1's 1,204 hours buying, and for whom?

13. Going deeper

PM interviews places this stage inside its loop, the only level at which incremental validity can be argued. PRD structure matters next: a take-home is only as good as the artefact it asks for. A PM's operating system and Continuous learning as a PM explain why someone who writes well under pressure has a system, not a talent. Building a PM portfolio and narrative unlocks the alternative route: two publishable teardowns let a candidate decline a take-home and still be taken seriously. Transitioning into product management is where the format bites hardest of all. Your first 90 days in a PM role closes the loop, since Table 6's rating comes out of those ninety days. And Confidence, doubt and judgement is the construct the instrument reaches for and most often misses.
case20v1-craft.interview.takehome:
Ninety-Six Hours at Abhiyaan Cargo Exchange

A case on written take-homes, PRDs and teardowns

1. Opening

At 6:04 pm on Thursday, 9 October 2025, Aarushi Banerjee sat in a Powai co-working space and read an email for the third time. She was a senior associate at a Mumbai strategy consultancy, a 2022 graduate of ISB, earning ₹24 lakh a year, and she had spent four months trying to move into product management. The email came from Arvind Bhalla, Head of Product at Abhiyaan Cargo Exchange in Gurugram. It confirmed that she had cleared the phone screen for an Associate Product Manager role, offering ₹28 lakh fixed and ₹4 lakh variable, and it attached a written assignment due on Monday, 13 October, at 6:00 pm. That gave her exactly 96 hours.

The assignment was one paragraph long. It ended with a sentence she could not stop reading: "There is no page limit." The note above it said the company expected the exercise to take about eight hours. She had perhaps twenty-five hours she could realistically find. What she did with them, and what she chose to hand in, was the decision in front of her.

2. Company background

Abhiyaan Cargo Exchange, founded in 2019, runs a digital marketplace that matches shippers with independent truck operators. Its shippers are mostly FMCG distributors, paint and building-material dealers and mid-sized manufacturers. Its supply side is roughly 41,000 registered fleet owners, most of whom own fewer than five trucks. In the year to March 2025 the exchange moved freight worth ₹1,800 crore and kept a take rate of 4.5 per cent, which is revenue of ₹81 crore.

The competitive set is crowded. BlackBuck is the best-known brand among truckers; Porter dominates intra-city loads; Delhivery and Rivigo approach the same shippers with owned or contracted capacity. Abhiyaan's argument is trust and settlement: e-way bills under GST are generated inside the app, FASTag data confirms movement, and a photographed proof of delivery closes each trip. It is the settlement step that hurts. Shippers pay Abhiyaan thirty days after delivery, and fleet owners, who pay for diesel and tolls in cash, say they wait fifteen to twenty-five days for their balance.

3. The situation

The assignment asked Aarushi to write a product requirements document proposing how Abhiyaan should shorten that wait. It listed three constraints: two engineers, one quarter, and no change to the thirty-day terms agreed with shippers.

She knew from Arvind that Abhiyaan's last round, in August and September, had been heavy. She did not know the rubric, or what a strong submission looked like. She had never worked in logistics.

Bhavya Agnihotri, an ISB classmate now a product manager at a marketplace in Warsaw, told her to go big. "They said no page limit. Show range: personas, a competitive matrix, a full roadmap, mock-ups. I did fourteen pages for my last one and got the offer." Brijesh Arora, a product lead on Abhiyaan's payments team who works from Amsterdam and reads submissions at night after his own day, sent a two-line reply through a mutual contact: "Please do not make us read twenty pages. Tell us what you would do first and why."

The two pieces of advice pointed in opposite directions, and both came from people who knew the process. Figure 1 shows the clock she was working against.

4. The people

Aarushi Banerjee, 28, Mumbai, is the candidate. She wants the role, a 33 per cent rise on her current ₹24 lakh (the offer's ₹32 lakh is ₹8 lakh higher), and a way into product without a prior PM title. Her instinct is to over-deliver.

Arvind Bhalla, Head of Product, Gurugram, designed the assignment. He wants to find out whether a candidate can choose, not whether she can produce volume.

Brijesh Arora, Amsterdam, is the second reviewer. He reads on a phone and in a different time zone, and he wants the recommendation in the first page.

Bhavya Agnihotri, Warsaw, is Aarushi's friend and her mentor in this process. Her advice rests on one success, which she treats as a rule.

5. Exhibits

Arvind agreed on the phone to share anonymised numbers from the last round. Exhibit 1 shows what happened. Of 200 candidates invited, 140 submitted, a completion rate of 70 per cent. Two reviewers shortlisted 21 of those 140 for an on-site loop, which is 15.0 per cent of submissions and 10.5 per cent of invitations. The exhibit classifies the other 119 by the single main reason a reviewer gave for rejection.

6. The options

Option A: the full PRD. Write twelve to fourteen pages covering personas, a competitive matrix, a roadmap and mock-ups, as Bhavya advised. It would show range and use 20 of her 25 hours (Exhibit 3). The cost is the pattern in Exhibit 2: documents of nine pages or more were shortlisted at 5.3 per cent. With no priority and a quarter's engineering capacity of only two people, it risks the scope-sprawl failure.

Option B: a focused memo. Spend the first hours on two phone calls with fleet owners she can reach through a Delhi transporter acquaintance and a short list of written questions to Arvind. Then write four pages that open with a recommendation, define the problem in one paragraph, choose a single bet, state two or three assumptions, name one metric with a counter-metric and say what she would cut. This uses 10 hours, closer to the stated eight, and aims at the failures in Exhibit 1. The cost is that it looks thin beside a fourteen-page rival and gives her fewer chances to display breadth.

Option C: a prototype-led submission. Build a clickable flow of an "instant payout" screen in four hours and attach a two-page note. It makes the idea vivid and uses only 11 hours. The cost is that a prototype can hide thin reasoning, and the assignment asked for a document.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What is Arvind trying to learn about a candidate by leaving the length unlimited, and how does Exhibit 1 change your answer?
  2. Bhavya's fourteen pages won an offer, while the round's data shows long submissions losing. How should Aarushi weigh one success against 140 observations, and what does Exhibit 2 not prove?
  3. Which of the six failure modes in Exhibit 1 is Aarushi most exposed to given that she has never worked in logistics, and which option guards best against it?
  4. If you were Arvind, would you change the assignment, the rubric or the information you share with candidates? What would you measure next time?

8. A note for the learner

A take-home is a work sample of judgement under constraint. The reader is a tired colleague, so what is being tested is whether the writer can decide what matters, say what she does not know and make a recommendation someone could act on. The topic's central idea is that a reviewable exercise is built for a reviewer: it leads with the answer, defines one problem, makes explicit what is assumed and measurable, and respects the stated constraints. Most failures are failures of omission, not of polish.

One defensible path is Option B. The round's own data points that way: the two biggest failures (problem undefined, no metric) are errors of thinking that extra pages do not repair, and the stated constraint of two engineers and one quarter forces a choice that a roadmap would dodge. Brijesh's message is also the closest evidence of what a reader wants. Her calls should replace invented data with sourced data, itself a failure in Exhibit 1.

A good memo might recommend one payout step the two engineers can ship within ninety days without touching the thirty-day shipper terms, for example advancing part of the balance against a confirmed proof of delivery, funded through a lending partner, with a stated fee and an eligibility test. Its metric might be median days from delivery to payment, with repeat-trip rate as counter-metric. It should then state plainly what she would not build, and what she would check first.

Option A is not wrong in principle, only mismatched with this reviewer and this evidence. Option C would be reasonable if the role were design-heavy. Whichever she chooses, Aarushi should send Arvind two clarifying questions on Friday morning and list any unanswered ones as assumptions. Asking costs almost nothing.
case20v1-craft.interview.loop:
The PM interview loop, stage by stage

A teaching case on preparation, targeting and who actually decides

1. Opening

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, in the library at the Indian School of Business in Hyderabad, Gauri Bhandari opened three calendar invitations side by side. Each was from a different company, each was for a product management role, and each carried a date within the next seventeen days. She had cleared the recruiter screen at all three. What stood between her and an offer was everything after it.

She had sixty hours of preparation she could realistically spend before 20 October, about four hours a day across fifteen days, once classes, group assignments and sleep were counted. The Garuda Mobility Network recruiter had also written that the 16 October slot would be released to another candidate unless Gauri confirmed it by five o'clock on Thursday 8 October. That was the deadline. By then she had to decide how to spend the sixty hours, and therefore whether all three loops were worth keeping.

2. Company background

Gauri was twenty-nine. She had spent four years as a software engineer at an IT services firm in Pune, the kind of employer that sits in the same conversation as Infosys and TCS, and had joined the one-year programme at ISB to move into product. She carried an education loan of ₹41 lakh.

Gagan Commerce Exchange, based in Bengaluru, runs a business-to-business marketplace that connects 3.4 lakh neighbourhood retailers with FMCG distributors. It competes for retailer attention with Udaan and with Reliance Retail's JioMart partner network,. Bhoomi Payments Systems, in Gurugram, serves 14 lakh small merchants with QR codes and speaker-box devices on UPI rails run by NPCI under RBI oversight, and it competes with PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay for the same shop counters. Garuda Mobility Network, in Pune, operates 2,300 charging points for electric two-wheelers and is a smaller, younger company; its rivals include Ather's own charging grid and the Ola Electric ecosystem.

3. The situation

Gauri's first instinct was to treat each loop as a set of independent exams. She spoke to three people who saw the process from different places.

Gunjan Bhatt, the recruiter at Gagan, explained that the first call filters on basics and pay expectations. The hiring manager conversation, she said, is where the manager decides whether to spend a scarce headcount on this person. The four onsite interviews produce written feedback, each filed separately. A "bar raiser" from another team, Greta Bjorklund in Stockholm, joins the final debrief by video and holds a veto.

Bhaskar Ghosal, an ISB alumnus working as a product manager in Melbourne, told Gauri over a late call that the loop is a chain rather than a set of exams: the stories she tells the hiring manager on day one reappear, in someone else's notes, in the debrief on day ten. Contradictions between rounds, he said, sink more candidates than a weak answer in one round.

Garima Bakshi, who coaches candidates at ISB's Career Advancement Office, had seen students who split their effort evenly arrive at every loop under-prepared for the first live conversation.

Exhibit 1 sets out the calendar. The three loops overlap, so every day of preparation counts for more than one company.

4. The people

Gauri Bhandari, the candidate, in Hyderabad, wants the strongest first product role she can earn and cannot afford a bare-handed first loop. Gunjan Bhatt, recruiter at Gagan in Gurugram, wants candidates who do not waste the hiring manager's time. Greta Bjorklund, the bar raiser, sits in Stockholm and wants the company's standard to hold; her 3 p.m. debrief slot falls at 6.30 in the evening in India. Bhaskar Ghosal in Melbourne wants his juniors to stop treating the loop as a quiz. Garima Bakshi in Hyderabad wants every student to leave with a schedule.

5. The evidence

Garima shared anonymised outcomes from last year's ISB cohort, counted from the hiring manager stage onward. Exhibit 2 shows what each stage eliminated and who made the call.

Two patterns stand out. At every firm the hiring manager conversation removed at least 50 per cent of those who reached it, the largest single cut at Garuda and tied for the largest at Gagan and Bhoomi. And the later stages mostly confirm or contest what that person concluded. Compounding the three stages, Gagan converted 16 of 80, or 20.0 per cent; Bhoomi 9 of 48, or 18.75 per cent; Garuda 12 of 40, or 30.0 per cent.

Exhibit 3 puts the pay on the table. The figures are annual cost to company in ₹ lakh, and the final column weights each by the cohort conversion rate above. It is a crude guide and not a forecast, because Gauri's own odds differ from the cohort's.

Garuda scores highest on this measure and Gagan second, yet Gauri's own preference ran in the other direction: Gagan offered the most learning and the strongest name on a first product résumé. The weighted figures showed only that none of the three was a poor use of her time.

6. The options

Option 1: Spread the time evenly. Twenty hours for each company. It keeps all three loops alive and avoids any irreversible choice. The cost is that each loop gets a third of her effort, prepared in isolation, which is how contradictions creep in.

Option 2: Go all in on Gagan. Forty-five hours for Gagan, fifteen for Bhoomi, and withdraw from Garuda before Thursday. This puts 75 per cent of her hours behind the company she wants most, and it removes the most crowded week in the calendar. The cost is that she gives up the loop with the best cohort conversion rate, and if the Gagan hiring manager says no on 12 October, she has little left for the loop two days later.

Option 3: Prepare by stage, not by company. Spend thirty hours on a shared core, meaning her stories, the "why this role" conversation, and product sense and metrics reasoning that all three hiring managers will probe. Then add firm-specific top-ups of twelve hours for Gagan, ten for Bhoomi and eight for Garuda. This aims at the stage that eliminates most people and keeps her stories consistent. The cost is that no loop gets a deep rehearsal of its own quirks, and the bar raiser round may be under-rehearsed.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. At each of the three firms, who is actually deciding at each stage, and what is each stage testing that the previous one did not?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about where preparation changes the outcome most, and what does it not tell you about Gauri in particular?
  3. Exhibit 3 ranks Garuda first and Gagan second. Why might Gauri reasonably discount that ranking, and what would you want to know before trusting it?
  4. Which option would you choose before 5 p.m. on 8 October, what would make you change it after 12 October, and what would you tell Garuda?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is that an interview loop is a sequence of different decisions made by different people, not one long exam. The hiring manager conversation decides whether to spend a headcount. The onsite rounds generate independent evidence. The debrief, with or without a bar raiser, resolves conflicts in that evidence.

A well-reasoned answer starts from Exhibit 2, not from the brand names. The hiring manager conversation is the largest or equal-largest cut at every firm, and it is the stage every preparation hour can reach, because it draws on the same stories and the same product reasoning regardless of company.

One defensible path is Option 3. It concentrates thirty of the sixty hours, half her time, on the shared core that is tested first at every firm. The top-ups are ordered by when each loop begins and by how much that firm's final stage differs: twelve hours for Gagan because of the bar raiser, ten for Bhoomi, eight for Garuda. She confirms the 16 October slot with Garuda before the deadline, since the weighted figures show it is worth keeping, and it also gives her a rehearsal for the later loops. Option 1 treats unlike stages as alike. Option 2 buys depth by giving up the loop with the best cohort conversion rate, and it exposes her to a single bad conversation.

The path has a trigger. If the Gagan hiring manager passes her on 12 October, she moves some hours into the Gagan onsite. If not, her shared-core work is already in use for the other two.
case40v1-craft.interview.loop:
Rule 11 and the Thursday debrief

Hiranya Payments Network, Bengaluru — a case on what each stage of a product hiring loop tests, and who actually decides

1. Sunday night, 4 October 2026

A quarter past eleven. Three documents lay on Oindrila Hegde's table in Indiranagar: a debrief scorecard for a candidate named Harini Hampiholi, a note filed the previous morning by an interviewer who had voted against her, and clause 11 of the hiring charter Hiranya Payments Network's board people committee approved in August 2023.

Oindrila was Vice President, Product. Fifty-four product managers sat in her organisation, eleven seats were open, and the plan she would take to the board on Friday 16 October assumed all eleven filled by March. On Thursday a five-person debrief had split: three positives, one clear negative, the standing bar raiser not inclined. Under clause 11.2 that ends the candidacy. The rejection had not gone out: Harini's hiring manager refused to let it.

Harini held a written offer from Hindola Commerce Exchange that lapsed at six on Tuesday evening. At nine on Monday Oindrila's head of talent would want a decision — and a verdict on whether the nine-stage loop that produced this split was worth keeping. She had read the scorecard four times, and was less and less certain it was about Harini at all.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Hiranya Payments Network was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by Hridaan Oswal and two classmates, selling QR acceptance to kirana stores one street at a time. Ten years on it served 11.4 lakh merchants, processed ₹1.86 lakh crore of payments in FY26 and reported revenue of ₹1,480 crore. Since 2023 it had also been a Lending Service Provider, disbursing ₹3,100 crore in FY26 through partner NBFCs under the Reserve Bank's digital lending framework. Of its 2,900 people, product sat in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Dublin, data science in Vancouver and commercial in Bangkok, serving a licensing deal in São Paulo and a lending pilot in Nairobi.

The constraint on Monday predated Oindrila. In 2023, after a senior product hire went badly and two quarters of roadmap were lost rebuilding what that person had shipped, Hridaan asked the people committee for a brake. Clause 11 created the bar raiser: a director-level product leader from outside the hiring team who reads every piece of written feedback and attends every debrief. Clause 11.2 gave that person a veto; 11.4 let the chief executive override one twice in a financial year; 11.6 allowed a re-interview on material new evidence. Amendments needed the committee, which met next on Friday 20 November. Both overrides were spent — February and September, each a Pune hire Hridaan wanted personally.

3. The market for merchants, and the market for product managers

Hiranya competed for counter space with PhonePe, Paytm, Google Pay and Razorpay on rails run by NPCI under RBI supervision, in a market where the person-to-merchant transaction carried no merchant discount rate. Revenue came from devices, subscriptions, settlement and lending distribution, so decisions about onboarding friction and underwriting were the business. The DPDP Act had made every data-processing contract a live question, and RBI's tightening of the lending rules had forced two roadmap rewrites.

The market for the people who made those decisions was tighter. Hiranya hired against Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, Meesho, Zerodha, Groww, Postman and Freshworks; Hitaishi Search Services, its retained firm in Gurugram, reported that payments-experienced candidates ran two to four processes at once and closed within three weeks. Hindola Commerce Exchange had hired four product managers from Hiranya's rejection pile in a year; one, Oviya Honavar, was declined at the assessment stage in March 2026 with a score of 52 and by September had shipped Hindola's merchant onboarding revamp — a fact Harsha Hublikar, Hiranya's director of talent acquisition, put on the first slide of every hiring review since.

4. The situation in detail

Exhibit 1 sets out the loop as it stood in October 2026: nine stages, each with a nominal decider.

Three things had happened in six weeks, each believed to mean something other than what it now appears to mean. In April the organisation was given a plan of twenty-four product hires for the first half of FY27; by 30 September it had closed fifteen. Harsha's diagnosis all summer was speed, and Exhibit 3 was built to carry it: on 22 September Hitaishi sent a pack showing a market median of twenty-one days from application to offer against Hiranya's forty-four, and Harsha circulated it under the subject line 23 days of self-harm.

On 29 September, Oorja Hiremath in Vancouver circulated an analysis of her own. The largest loss of candidates the hiring manager already wanted came at stage 4: of 240 assessments issued in the half-year, 90 were never completed and 30 more did not clear, so 120 of 240 survived. And on the 2025 cohort the score carried no usable relationship to how people were rated a year later — a rank correlation of −0.08 across the nineteen hires with a twelve-month rating. The highest score Hiranya had recorded, 94, belonged to Hrishikesh Halbe, rated 2 at review; the other three in his band averaged 3.73. Harita Hosmane, hired by exception in February 2025 below the pass mark because Hridaan insisted, was rated 4.3.

Then, on Monday 28 September, Harini Hampiholi came onsite: thirty-one, an ISB graduate, a product manager at Odhani Retail Works. Her assessment score was 71 — the band that in Exhibit 4 rates highest among those who cleared. Her loop, in the upper panel of Exhibit 6, took fifty-eight days to reach the debrief on Thursday 1 October, twenty-six of them between grading and onsite against a stage median of eleven.

The debrief ran at 6.30 p.m. in Bengaluru, 2 p.m. in Dublin and 6 a.m. in Vancouver. Hitendra Ohri, the bar raiser, declared himself not inclined, citing execution. The written detail behind the negative vote he relied on reached the tracking system on Saturday 3 October, two days later.

5. The people

Oindrila Hegde, VP Product, Bengaluru. Wants the bar held and the calendar shortened, which she knows is two wants. Carries Q4 commitments made on eleven filled seats. Has not told the board she doubts the charter can be amended before 20 November.

Harsha Hublikar, director of talent acquisition, Bengaluru. Wants five stages, no assessment, the bar raiser as adviser; is measured on time-to-fill and offer-accept, both failing. Does not mention that her recruiters reject three of every four candidates who reach the screen, a stage nobody audits.

Hemal Ozarkar, group product manager, Pune, hiring manager for the merchant-credit seat. Says Harini is the strongest candidate in four months and the veto is wrong; has carried two unfilled roles since June and is blamed for his team's slips. Does not mention that Hindola has approached him twice, or that in those eighty-one minutes he described the credit roadmap in detail — material she then used fluently in two later rounds.

Hitendra Ohri, director of product, lending, Bengaluru, one of three standing bar raisers. Says the loop produced no evidence she had been accountable for a hard trade-off, and absent that the bar says no; the 2023 episode happened on his watch, and the charter is in a sense his. Does not mention that he formed his view before the detailed negative feedback was filed, from a card on which nobody owned execution, or that he is in Warsaw from 5 to 9 October.

Hansa Okhade, director of engineering, Pune, onsite round 2. Says Harini sat on a ₹6.4 crore reconciliation backlog for eleven weeks at Odhani and froze a launch for five weeks rather than escalating; sits on four loops a month and resents it. Does not mention that she asked the question Hemal had asked and scored it 2 where he scored 3, neither knowing.

Hiranmay Oturkar, principal designer, Dublin, onsite round 3. Rates her stakeholder craft the best in the pipeline and wants design to have a vote on product hires. Read Hemal's notes before his round, which the charter discourages.

Oorja Hiremath, staff data scientist, Vancouver, onsite round 1. Says the problem is measurement, not length, and wants her analysis adopted and the vendor contract killed. Joined the debrief at 6 a.m., spoke for ninety seconds and filed the shortest feedback on the card.

Hridaan Oswal, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Created the bar raiser and will not dismantle it in a quarter when product is behind plan; faces a Series F conversation in which hiring discipline is a talking point. Both overrides this year went to people he had met socially.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 3 framed the summer's debate. Its last row sums eight stage medians rather than taking the median of eight totals.

Exhibit 4 is Oorja's, and the most fragile table in the pack.

Exhibit 5 prices the loop. What Oindrila returned to was the hours: 1,904 in six months, about 35 per product manager.

Exhibit 6 is the document on her table.

7. Voices

"Nine of the twenty-four finalists we approved this half-year declined us, and every one of them cited our timeline. Twenty-three days slower than the market is not a bar, it is a tax."

— Harsha Hublikar, email to Oindrila Hegde and Hridaan Oswal, 22 September 2026

"Nobody in that room was responsible for finding out whether she can execute. So four of us each found out a quarter of it, and then we averaged our ignorance."

— Hemal Ozarkar, product leadership channel, 2 October 2026

"The question is whether this loop produced evidence that she has owned a hard trade-off and can defend it. It did not. If I wave that through because a seat is open, clause 11 means nothing by December."

— Hitendra Ohri, debrief recording, 1 October 2026

"For the record: I asked her about the ₹6.4 crore reconciliation. She froze a launch for five weeks and did not take it to her VP. Hemal heard the same story and scored it a three. One of us is wrong and the scorecard cannot tell you which."

— Hansa Okhade, note filed to the ATS, 3 October 2026

8. The options, as Oindrila saw them on Sunday night

Uphold the veto. Harini is declined on Monday, Harsha releases the two other finalists, and clause 11 keeps its force. The cost is a hiring manager, already approached twice by a competitor, who will read it as a ruling that his judgement does not count, and a seat open into its fifth month.

Seek an override. Clause 11.4 is spent for the year. The only lawful route to reopen the candidacy is 11.6, material new evidence — and the only document filed since Thursday is Hansa Okhade's note, which argues against Harini. Oindrila could call it new evidence precisely because it shows two interviewers judging the same episode differently: a negative document as the trigger for a second look. Hitendra is in Warsaw until 9 October; the offer lapses on Tuesday at six.

Re-run one round. A single ninety-minute execution interview with a named decider — herself — on Monday evening. It answers the competency the loop never assigned. It also looks exactly like what a hiring manager gets when he shouts loudly enough, and matches no stage in Exhibit 1.

Rebuild the loop and let this candidate go. Serve ninety days' notice on Ojaswi, accept the ₹6.75 lakh termination payment, replace stage 4 with a forty-five-minute working session inside the onsite day, assign one competency to each round in writing, and ask the people committee to turn the veto into a written objection the VP must answer on the record. Target: twenty-four days end to end. None of it can be done before Tuesday.

Each answers the question she had been asking since September: speed, or the bar. On Sunday she noticed that neither Exhibit 2 nor Exhibit 6 was about either. Three of every four candidates who reached the recruiter screen were rejected by a stage no product manager had audited; forty-eight debriefs produced twelve hiring-manager-versus-bar-raiser splits, half of all rejections there; and a card of fifteen scores averaged exactly 3.00 because four people assessed four overlapping things and none was told which was theirs.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday 5 October, 9 a.m.: Harsha wants the Harini decision and the loop verdict. Tuesday 6 October, 6 p.m.: the Hindola offer lapses. Friday 16 October: the board review. Friday 20 November: the people committee, the only body that can amend clause 11.

Money and contracts. The Ojaswi agreement runs to 31 March 2027 with a minimum of 600 graded assessments per contract year at ₹2,500 each, or ₹15.00 lakh; 150 were used in the first half, implying 300 for the year and a ₹7.50 lakh shortfall payment if nothing changes. Early exit requires ninety days' notice and 60 per cent of the unconsumed minimum: ₹15.00 lakh less the ₹3.75 lakh consumed, at 60 per cent, is ₹6.75 lakh. Legal has flagged that the contract predates the DPDP rules and that vendor-held submissions need fresh consent language.

People and pay. Eleven open seats at the band midpoint of ₹42 lakh commit ₹4.62 crore a year; the approved incremental budget for the second half of FY27 is ₹2.31 crore, exactly half of it, leaving nothing for exceptions. The senior product manager ceiling is ₹46 lakh. Harini's cost to company is ₹38 lakh; her ask, and Hindola's offer, is ₹49 lakh. Anything above ₹46 lakh needs Hridaan's signature at stage 9.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Walk through Exhibit 1: what does each stage test that the previous one did not, and who genuinely decides at each, as distinct from who the charter says decides?
  2. Exhibit 3 was built to prove the loop too slow, Exhibit 4 to prove one stage worthless. Read each against its footnotes: what must be true for either to carry its weight?
  3. Exhibit 6 shows fifteen scores averaging exactly 3.00. Is that a finding about the candidate, about the loop's design, or about averaging independent judgements?
  4. Harsha Hublikar's email and the exit notes in Exhibit 2 disagree about why nine finalists declined. Whose account would you test first, and how, before 16 October?
  5. Clause 11 was meant to prevent a repeat of 2023. It now accounts for half of all debrief rejections, across three bar raisers who disagree about how often they use it. Is it doing that job, and how would you know?
  6. It is nine on Monday morning. What does Oindrila do about Harini Hampiholi, what does she do about the loop, and what goes on the slide for 16 October — including what she tells the board she got wrong?

11. Later that night

At twenty past midnight Oindrila drafted a message to Hemal and did not send it. She drafted a second to Hitendra in Warsaw, asking whether his position would change if he knew two interviewers had scored the same story differently, and did not send that either. The scorecard lay where it had lain all evening, fifteen numbers averaging to the exact middle of the scale, and she could not decide whether she held a verdict on a candidate, an audit of her own organisation, or a form nine stages had filled in that nobody had been asked to sign.
exp40v2-craft.interview.loop:
The PM interview loop, stage by stage

Recruiter screen, hiring manager, onsite rounds, bar raiser, debrief — what each tests, who holds the decision, and why almost every loop in use is tuned for precision at the expense of recall

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On Thursday 1 October 2026 in Mumbai, Prashant Kanitkar, Director of Product at Parvat Payments Network, reviewed the 183 days from 1 April to 30 September 2026: 3,200 product-management applications in, 14 people on the payroll out. Poornima Kashyap, the chief product officer, had one question before approving 26 more hires: was the loop selecting, or only filtering?

A memo from Kavita Puranik, Parvat's talent lead, listed candidates the loop turned away in 2025 who by late 2026 held comparable or more senior roles elsewhere. One was Kalpana Pargaonkar, held in March 2025 by Pramod Kelshikar, the principal PM who serves as Parvat's bar raiser, for thin evidence of influence without authority. Parvat had priced every post-onsite rejection at zero, never hearing of them again.

On Monday 28 September 2026 in Bengaluru, Keerthana Palepu faced the mirror image. Palepu, 31, a Senior PM at Kshipra Commerce Collective on ₹48 lakh cost-to-company, was live in two loops: Pradhaan Treasury Works, a Chennai firm selling treasury software to banks, which opened her file on 14 September and set six stages with an onsite on 26 October, 42 days later; and Kaveri Intelligence Labs, a 40-person Pune document-intelligence firm, which screened her on 22 September and offered five. She had 34 days to 1 November and about 60 spare hours.

Both are asking one question from opposite chairs, and both answers turn on a single fact: a loop is not a measuring instrument but a sequence of asymmetric decision rights, and almost every PM loop in use is tuned to avoid the wrong hire rather than find the right one. That is defensible for a firm that can wait, expensive for one that cannot, and no stage tells you which you are.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A loop is an ordered sequence of assessments, each owned by a named person, each ending in a written verdict, with a rule for aggregating them into one decision. The recruiter screen tests level, band, mobility and motivation; the hiring-manager screen is the first conversation with whoever will own the hire's output; the onsite assigns one competency and one interviewer per round; the debrief pools the verdicts and applies the rule. The bar raiser, from outside the hiring team, compares the candidate against everyone hired at that level rather than this cycle's field — a role Amazon institutionalised in the 1990s.

The loop solves a documented problem: one impressed interviewer predicts performance badly. Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 meta-analysis put structured-interview validity at .51 against .38 for unstructured conversation and .54 for a work sample; Sackett and colleagues, correcting for range restriction in 2022, reported .42 and .33. The direction survived — structure beats conversation — but the magnitudes shrank, and with them any claim that a loop is precise. Google's analysis, reported by Laszlo Bock in 2015, found four interviewers captured about 86 per cent of the confidence any larger panel would reach, turning the question into which four, deciding what. Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein named the discipline in 2021: independent judgement first, aggregation second.

Three schools disagree substantively. Structure maximalists will sign that every round maps to one competency scored against a rubric, that verdicts are filed before the debrief, and that a bar raiser holds a veto; they will not sign that more rounds produce more signal. Minimalists will sign that two deep conversations plus a paid work sample beat five interviews, since the loop's cost falls on the candidate; they will not sign that a committee is a safeguard. Recall advocates, Puranik's position, will sign that a loop's false-reject rate is its most important unmeasured statistic; they will not sign that a conservative loop is safe.

3. Mechanics in depth: decision rights, then arithmetic

Practitioners describe a loop as a list of rounds. Experts describe it as a distribution of two non-interchangeable rights: the right to stop a candidate and the right to advance one.

Table 1. The Parvat PM loop as decision rights, October 2026. “Stop”: the stage can end the candidacy alone. “Advance”: it can carry the candidate to an offer alone.
StageOwnerCan stopCan advanceError it cannot catch
Recruiter screen: level, band, motivationKavita PuranikYesNoScope presented badly
Hiring-manager screen: past ownershipPrashant KanitkarYesNoIts own warmth; he is also selling
Onsite 1: product sense and craftPriyal KamerkarNoNoJudgement under real constraints
Onsite 2: execution and analyticsKartikeya PingleNoNoWork done through others
Onsite 3: technical fluencyKiran ParulekarNoNoPayments-regulation depth
Onsite 4: bar raiser, level calibrationPramod KelshikarYes (hold)NoIts own conservatism; holds go unaudited
Debrief: the written record onlyKanitkar chairsYesRecommendCandidates who never reached it
Offer approval: level and bandPoornima KashyapYesYesEverything; evidence is already fixed

Five of eight stages can end a candidacy alone; exactly one can create an offer. The bias that follows is independent of interviewer quality: errors of commission meet five filters, errors of omission none. The onsite rounds hold neither right — they produce evidence, which is why their write-ups are filed before the debrief, not argued inside it.

An applicant's unconditional chance of an offer was 20 in 3,200, or 0.625 per cent; one who reached the onsite faced 20 in 96, or 20.83 per cent. Only the second is worth planning with.

The arithmetic nobody runs

The loop also costs 1,346.8 interviewer and recruiter hours a half-year, of which onsite and debrief take 720, or 53.5 per cent: at a blended ₹3,500 an hour, ₹47,13,800, which is ₹3,36,700 for each of the 14 hires. Kanitkar then tried to fill all four cells, not the two hiring data supplies. For precision he used performance: of the 14 joiners, 11 were rated at or above the level bar at 12 months, 78.6 per cent. Applied to the 24 recommended, 24 × 11 ÷ 14 = 18.86, rounded to 19 above the bar and 5 below. For the invisible cell, Puranik traced the 72 rejected after an onsite and established the later trajectory of 58, or 80.6 per cent of them; of those 58, 23 had by late 2026 reached a level at or above the one Parvat declined them for. That is 39.7 per cent, which applied to all 72 gives 28.55, rounded to 29.

The implied base rate is 48 of 96, exactly 50 per cent. Precision, the share above the bar among those the loop said yes to, is 19 ÷ 24 = 79.2 per cent. Specificity, the share correctly declined among those below, is 43 ÷ 48 = 89.6 per cent. Sensitivity, the share found among those above, is 19 ÷ 48 = 39.6 per cent. Negative predictive value is 43 ÷ 72 = 59.7 per cent: two in five rejections were wrong.

Every choice that raises specificity — an extra veto, a higher threshold, a convention that ambiguity means no — lowers sensitivity, and the loop reports only the first. Parvat's loop is tuned for a firm that would rather miss three good candidates than hire one weak one, and nobody there decided that.

4. When the loop's logic holds, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions carry the case for a multi-stage loop. First: a mis-hire costs more than a miss. Kanitkar estimates a weak senior hire at 1.2 times cost-to-company against another cycle of the funnel; it holds weakly. At Kaveri, where one PM covers an entire model-facing surface, a three-month vacancy is worse than an imperfect hire, so the condition fails and a veto is wrong.

Second: the competencies are separable, since a loop adds information only if its rounds observe different things. Parvat's four rounds pass on paper; only correlating scores settles it, which Parvat had never done. Third: the market tolerates the elapsed time. Parvat's median loop ran 29 days, which its brand carries; Kaveri's ran 41, which its candidates would not. Fourth: there is a history to calibrate against, failing which the bar raiser is one person's taste.

The idea misleads in two places: the founder-led hire for a role that does not yet exist, where the premise that competencies are known in advance is false; and the internal transfer, where five rounds swap four hours of inference for four years of evidence. For Palepu, Pradhaan's loop is a filter with six gates, Kaveri's a negotiation with three people she can persuade.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Loops break at joins. In multi-product firms the question is whether the bar raiser sits in the hiring team's unit. Parvat runs three: collections, payouts and a nascent lending platform. Kelshikar sits in collections, and 8 of his 11 holds were on payouts and lending candidates — rigour, or unfamiliarity.

In two-sided and platform businesses the rounds test the side the interviewers know: Parvat's product-sense round was written from the merchant side, and candidates reasoning from the acquiring bank's position scored poorly for “missing the user”. In regulated sectors — Kshem Insurance Services is the clearest case — a compliance round carries a veto, which is backwards: regulation is learnable in a quarter and judgement is not. In hardware-plus-software firms such as Pushkar Robotics Industries a firmware interviewer joins the loop, and is then allowed to judge priorities.

AI-native products create the newest seam. Kaveri's AI-fluency round tests reasoning about evaluation sets, failure taxonomies and the cost of a confidently wrong answer; it is the firm's most predictive round and the one interviewers disagree on most, because nobody has a distribution for a three-year-old competency. What mature firms do, rather than what their handbooks say, is route around the seam: a manager expecting a hold warns the candidate, pre-briefs that interviewer, or schedules the loop while he is away. None of this is written down.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

Stopping and advancing are different rights

Competent practitioners count rounds; experts count vetoes. Each stage that can stop a candidate multiplies survival by a number below one: five gates at 0.85 retain 44 per cent of acceptable candidates before anyone sees the work.

Low yield is a market statistic, not a quality statistic

Parvat's 0.4375 per cent end-to-end rate is read internally as a high bar; it is mostly an easy application form. The tell is a yield that fell while the accept rate held flat; post-onsite conversion, 20 in 96, is insensitive to volume.

A rejection and a hold are not the same decision

A screen rejection is almost never revisited; a debrief no-hire is reversible on new evidence; a hold needs Kashyap's written override. The tell is a firm logging all three as “rejected”, which is why Kelshikar's went unreviewed.

The hiring-manager screen is the only round with a conflict of interest

Kanitkar assesses the candidate and sells the job in one hour, and the second corrupts the first. The tell is a pass rate tracking how badly the team needs a body.

Independence is the mechanism, not a courtesy

The value of four verdicts is that they are four; the tell that independence has gone is verdicts clustering more tightly than the evidence justifies, or one interviewer's vocabulary in three.

A bar raiser calibrates against history; it does not vote

Its function is the comparison the hiring team cannot make, not a fifth opinion. The tell of drift is a hold phrased as preference: “I did not see enough” rather than “below our last twelve”.

The debrief weighs evidence; it does not average opinion

The tell is a decision reached by counting thumbs. A sound debrief reads each verdict, names the evidence behind each rating, and asks what one interviewer saw that another did not.

Every loop has a sensitivity figure, and almost no firm knows its own

Firms track time-to-hire, accept rate and regretted attrition, all ratios over people they hired; sensitivity needs information about those they did not. The tell is a review in which every metric is a ratio over joiners. A second is a decline rate rising with seniority: a long loop censors the top.

7. How the loop differs by product type and company stage

What genuinely differs is which competency the firm cannot teach, because that is what the loop must gate on. In consumer products it is judgement about users at volume, so product sense and analytics carry the weight. In B2B and enterprise software it is credibility with a buyer who is not the user, which is why Pradhaan gates on a treasury-domain round and why Palepu's weakest stage is her costliest to improve. In platforms and marketplaces it is holding two divergent customers in one decision, which rarely appears as a named round and is assessed inconsistently, as at Parvat. In hardware it is sequencing against a fixed tooling date; in AI, the price of confident error.

What does not differ is the recruiter screen, or the debrief, whose failure modes are identical across types. Stage matters more than type. A 40-person firm cannot run a bar raiser: no distribution to calibrate against, no interviewer to spare. A firm of 500 adds the role because its managers can no longer hold the standard in their heads. A firm of 5,000 finds it a bottleneck and trains a bench, at which point calibration decays toward taste unless holds are audited.

8. Three worked examples

Kshipra Commerce Collective compresses its loop

In 2025 Palepu's own employer cut its PM loop from six stages to four, dropping a product-sense round and the bar raiser. Median time-to-offer fell from 34 days to 19; the accept rate rose from 11 of 18 to 18 of 23, which is 61.1 per cent to 78.3 per cent. The cost appeared at 12 months: 1 of 11 joiners in the earlier cohort was below the level bar, 9.1 per cent; in the later cohort, 4 of 18, or 22.2 per cent. At ₹45 lakh cost-to-company and a mis-hire cost of 1.2 times that, ₹54 lakh, regret cost per hire rose from ₹54 lakh ÷ 11 = ₹4.91 lakh to 4 × ₹54 lakh ÷ 18 = ₹12.00 lakh, up ₹7.09 lakh. Against it, 15 days of avoided vacancy at ₹1.5 lakh a week saved ₹3.21 lakh. Net, compression cost ₹3.88 lakh per hire — arguably right before a festive quarter, but never argued as that trade.

Pradhaan Treasury Works adds a domain round

Pradhaan's PMs sell to bank treasuries. In 2022 to 2023, 9 of 24 PM hires were reassigned or departed within 12 months, 37.5 per cent. It added a 1.5-hour treasury-domain round; over the next two years, 3 of 21 hires left or were reassigned within 12 months, 14.3 per cent. At the earlier rate 21 hires would have produced 7.875 such outcomes, so the observed 3 implies 4.875 avoided at ₹35 lakh each, or ₹170.63 lakh — ₹1.71 crore. The round cost 86 onsite candidates × 1.5 hours = 129 hours at ₹3,000 an hour, ₹3.87 lakh — a return near 44 to 1, the signature of gating on something unteachable.

Where it failed: Kaveri Intelligence Labs imports a bar raiser

In early 2026 Kaveri's founder Pallav Kodiyeri added a bar-raiser veto, copied from a large firm two of his advisers had worked at. Kaveri had 40 people and two interviewers senior enough for it. The hours were trivial — 11 loops a month at 1.25 hours is 13.75 hours between two people — but the calendar was not: the median wait from onsite to a bar-raiser slot reached 11 days, and loop time rose to 41 days. Of 17 offers in two quarters, 6 were declined, 35.3 per cent, four citing elapsed time. The deeper failure was conceptual: with four PMs ever hired there was no distribution to calibrate against.

The recovery kept the function and dropped the mechanism: an adviser now reviews one loop in three after the offer has gone out and reports on drift quarterly. Loop time fell to 22 days and declines to 4 of 19, 21.1 per cent. Calibration became an audit rather than a gate — what a firm without a distribution can afford.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Rounds that correlate. Sign: verdicts agree almost perfectly. Diagnostic: across the last 50 candidates, which pair of round scores correlates above 0.7? Caught late, the firm paid for four rounds and bought one.

Rubric drift under pressure. Sign: “inclined to hire” verdicts rise after a headcount approval. Diagnostic: re-score ten write-ups from last year against this quarter's standard. Caught late, two cohorts sit at different levels under one title.

The debrief that is a vote. Sign: decisions in under 15 minutes with no reference to written evidence. Diagnostic: ask each interviewer which observation moved them, then check it appears in their pre-filed verdict. Caught late, the loop's variance is who spoke first.

The uncontested veto. Sign: one interviewer holds a disproportionate share, as Kelshikar did with 11 in 18 months. Diagnostic: how many of two years' holds were checked against what the candidate did next? Caught late, the bar belongs to one person's risk appetite.

Stage-purpose creep. Sign: the recruiter screen asks product questions, or approval reopens the decision. Diagnostic: name the question each stage settles; two stages answering one means a redundancy and a gap. Caught late, nobody can say where the decision is made.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a veto improve a loop? The maximalist's case is drift: a manager under pressure convinces himself, and the only counterweight is someone with no stake in the vacancy and authority to stop it. The evidence is the link between hiring urgency and verdict leniency. For it to be wrong, holds would have to be poorly calibrated — and Parvat's sensitivity of 39.6 per cent is that counter-evidence. The recall advocate replies that a veto is one-sided error correction: it shifts the loop toward false negatives, which, unmeasured, cannot be audited. For that to be wrong, a mis-hire must cost far more than a miss.

How many rounds? The minimalist holds that a paid work sample dominates any interview: it observes the actual work, and Sackett's corrected .33 is earned on a realistic task rather than a conversation about one. Against it, work samples are costly for employed candidates, exclude those with caring responsibilities, and get graded by whoever is free. The maximalist concedes Bock's diminishing returns but keeps a fifth round for a specific disagreement.

Who should decide? Manager sovereignty says the person who lives with the consequence should hold the call, since accountability without authority breeds defensive hiring. Committee sovereignty says managers over-weight similarity to themselves, and a committee reading only the record is less noisy. The comparison that would settle it, nobody runs.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied loops can name the stages. Someone who has internalised them asks first where the right to stop sits and where the right to advance sits, and treats that as the real specification; quotes conditional rather than unconditional probabilities, since 20 in 96 is actionable and 20 in 3,200 decorative; knows the loop's sensitivity or has a proxy; and separates calibration from gating, auditing after the fact where no distribution exists.

12. The two decisions

Kanitkar took three proposals to Kashyap on 2 October 2026. He kept Kelshikar's veto: one memo and a 39.6 per cent sensitivity estimate on a traced sample of 58 is suggestive, not conclusive. He converted it into a 48-hour written hold, in which Kelshikar must state the comparison to named past hires at the level and the hold lapses unless Kashyap confirms it. He commissioned a correlation study of the four onsite rounds. And he asked Puranik to extend the traced-rejects proxy to every later rejection, making Table 2's bottom row a standing measurement. Of the rounds, the rule and the measurement, only the third makes the others decidable.

Table 3 holds Palepu's own stage estimates, and what a block would do to each.

exp20v2-craft.interview.loop:
The PM interview loop, stage by stage

Who you meet at each stage, and what each one is actually deciding

1. Six seats, 480 applications

On Monday 5 October 2026, Bhaskar Dandavate, Director of Product at Dharti Mandi Collective, a Pune agricultural-produce marketplace, sat down with the chief product officer, Dipti Bhide. Between them lay the record of a hiring cycle that had opened on 6 July and ended with offers on 28 August, a span of 53 days. It had produced 480 applications for six Senior PM seats, and six people had joined. Each seat carried a cost-to-company of ₹48 lakh a year.

Dipti was uneasy about the debrief of 26 August. Four interviewers had met Devika Bhosale, a product manager from a fintech, and had split on her. The bar raiser, Balraj Dhillon, an interviewer from outside the hiring team whose job is to protect the company-wide standard, had tipped the decision. Across the cycle he had held three of the twelve candidates the panels recommended. Dipti proposed adding a fifth onsite round, a strategy case, so that no single voice carried that weight. Bhaskar had to say whether the loop was miscalibrated, or whether it was working as designed.

Figure 1 shows the shape of the cycle. Only 1.25 per cent of applicants joined, and most of the narrowing happened in the first two stages, before any senior interviewer had spent a full hour on anyone. The question Bhaskar faced was therefore not only whether to add a round, but what each existing stage was deciding, and who held the decision.

2. The idea

A loop is the sequence of conversations a company puts a PM candidate through, with each stage owned by a different person and designed to settle one question. Four stages repeat across most firms. The recruiter screen is a short call by a talent professional who checks basic fit, level, compensation expectations and motivation. The hiring manager screen is a conversation with the person who will manage the hire. The onsite is a set of back-to-back interviews, each testing a different skill, whether held in a building or on video. The debrief is the meeting where interviewers pool written evidence and decide. Many firms add a bar raiser, an interviewer drawn from outside the hiring team, with authority to block a hire, whose job is to keep the standard from sliding as hiring pressure rises. Amazon is widely credited with institutionalising the role in the early 2000s.

The loop was invented to solve a specific problem: one impressed interviewer is a poor predictor. Meta-analyses from the 1990s, notably Schmidt and Hunter's of 1998, found that structured interviews, where every candidate gets comparable questions scored against a rubric (a written scale describing what weak, adequate and strong answers look like), predicted job performance better than free conversation. A loop spreads the judgement across several people so that individual enthusiasm cancels out.

The sentence Bhaskar could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: each stage should decide one thing, and the loop works only when no stage is quietly asked to decide something that belongs to another.

3. How it actually works

Disha Bapat, the recruiter at Dharti, begins before any candidate speaks. She and Bhaskar agree the level, the compensation band and the competencies, then the recruiter screen tests the cheap questions: does the candidate's experience match the level, will the pay band hold, and why this role? The next stage is Bhaskar's own screen. He tests whether the candidate has handled problems of the right size and can describe a decision with its reasoning, and he is also selling the job, which tilts his judgement toward liking.

Table 1. The Dharti loop: who meets the candidate, what is tested, and who decides.
StageWho meets the candidateTestsWho decides
Recruiter screenDisha BapatLevel, pay band, motivationRecruiter, against a checklist
Hiring manager screenBhaskar DandavateScope of past work, clarity of reasoning, fit to roleHiring manager alone
Onsite, four roundsFour interviewers, one being the bar raiserProduct sense, execution and analytics, technical fluency, leadership behaviourNobody yet; each writes an independent verdict

Table 1 contains the steps practitioners usually leave implicit. Each interviewer must write the verdict before the debrief and before reading anyone else's, otherwise the first confident speaker anchors the room. The hiring manager owns the final recommendation, but at Dharti a bar raiser hold means an offer cannot proceed without Dipti's written override.

4. A worked example

Bhaskar rebuilt the cycle as a table. Each stage's hours equal the candidates it handled multiplied by the interviewer hours spent on each. The recruiter screen took 0.5 hour, the manager screen 0.75 hour, the onsite four one-hour rounds, and the debrief one hour for each of five attendees, which is 5 hours per candidate.

The fifth round breaks even if it prevents one mis-hire in every 72 ÷ 3.84 = 18.75 cycles, which is ₹0.64 lakh extra per hire (3.84 divided by 6), or 0.89 per cent of one ₹72 lakh mis-hire. The fifth round need only earn a small improvement in accuracy.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Early stages eliminate; they do not rank

The recruiter screen removed 360 of 480 candidates. Its purpose is to remove clear mismatches cheaply, not to pick the best.

The hiring manager is judge and seller

Bhaskar's screen tests competence while also persuading candidates to want the job. A warm conversation is weak evidence in either direction, and he should score it against the same competencies the onsite uses.

Independence is the mechanism

The loop's value comes from several separate observations. Interviewers who compare impressions in the corridor turn four observations into one.

A bar raiser calibrates; it does not add a vote

The bar raiser is confused with a senior fifth interviewer. The distinction is that the role compares this candidate against everyone the company has hired at that level, which a team under hiring pressure cannot do for itself.

Who decides depends on the firm

Some firms let the hiring manager decide, others use a committee, a few give a hold power to the bar raiser. Ask which model applies.

Table 3. Three kinds of “no” at Dharti.

A loop predicts imperfectly

Structured interviews beat unstructured ones, yet they remain predictions. They cannot show how someone performs with your engineers, your data and your politics.

Low yield does not mean a high bar

The 1.25 per cent join rate describes the funnel, not the quality of candidates or the rigour of the loop.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

Table 4. Where the loop's weight shifts.
SettingStage that carries most weightWhat changes
