Large firmDebrief and bar raiserMany interviewers, so the process guards against drift

Table 4 summarises a pattern that is real but not a rule. Consumer firms such as Swiggy or Flipkart run many loops a quarter, and so lean on rubrics for consistency. Dharti, as a marketplace, must test whether a candidate holds two customers in mind at once. A start-up with twenty people cannot afford a bar raiser, so one founder carries the whole decision, and the candidate's preparation should concentrate on that one person.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the debrief as a vote. The symptom is a decision reached by counting thumbs, with the loudest senior person winning. The misunderstanding is that the debrief averages opinions, when it exists to weigh evidence. The cheapest diagnostic is to read each written verdict before the meeting and ask which sentence of evidence supports each rating.

Asking every round the same thing. The symptom is that panel verdicts agree too closely, and candidates report four near-identical conversations. The misunderstanding is that more interviews mean more information. Assign each round one competency from Table 1, and check whether the verdicts still agree.

Using the hiring manager screen as a vibe check. The symptom is that candidates Bhaskar likes reach the onsite and later fail on basics. The misunderstanding is that likeability signals fit. The diagnostic is to compare the screen's score against the onsite results for the 48 who passed.

Adding rounds in reaction to one decision. The symptom is a loop that grows after each disagreement. The misunderstanding is that a hard case shows a missing stage rather than a calibration problem. Price the added round as in section 4 before approving it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the decision about Devika would have looked unremarkable. Her four interviewers would have written verdicts before they met, each citing evidence against its assigned competency. Balraj would have stated his hold in terms of the company's level standard rather than a feeling. Dipti would have read the file and either overridden it in writing or accepted it. Bhaskar would hold a record of why, which he could compare with her performance after twelve months. The target is a loop whose every stage can state its question.

9. Closing

Bhaskar told Dipti that he would not add the fifth round. The arithmetic was not decisive: ₹3.84 lakh per cycle is small beside ₹72 lakh. His reason was that the case against Balraj's hold was a single instance, and a fifth round would hide, rather than test, whether the three holds were right. He proposed two changes at no extra cost: written verdicts before the debrief, and a tracker comparing each of the six joiners' first-year performance against their round scores. If holds prove poor predictors, the loop changes; if good, the fifth round would add cost only.

The natural next topics are practising, through mocks, drills and feedback, which trains for each stage separately, and what to ask the interviewer, which turns the loop into a two-way test. Two questions to sit with. First, if you were Devika, which stage in Table 1 would you have prepared for least, and what is that choice costing you? Second, if you were Bhaskar, what evidence from a single cycle would be enough to change a loop, and what would be too little?
exp40v2-craft.pivot.narrative:
The career-switch narrative, at depth

Why most pivot stories fail before anyone reads them, what a hiring manager is actually doing in thirty-four seconds, and the evidence a switch has to carry.

1. Two decisions, four months apart

On 11 May 2026 in Coimbatore, Charulata Vaidya showed her résumé to Chirag Lalwani of Lagan Talent Services. She was 31, deputy manager for inspection software at Chakshu Vision Industries, a 470-person maker of machine-vision systems running on 88 auto-component lines, and earned ₹24 lakh. Since 6 April she had sent 31 applications for product roles and had one recruiter screen to show for it. Chirag read for a minute: the problem was not the writing but the thirty-one companies.

Three weeks later, on 1 June, she restarted with 34 firms in three archetypes: 14 selling software into manufacturing, 9 consumer applications, 11 horizontal business-software firms. Her decision was how to allocate a finite number of serious applications across them. By then she had sent 46 applications for 2 screens, a rate of 4.3 per cent.

Lokesh Chandavarkar had been at it longer, from another angle. He was 36, nine years in trade-finance operations at Vyapaar Settlement Systems, a 900-person Mumbai firm running reconciliation software for banks and exporters, on ₹46 lakh. On 18 February 2026 he called Vaishali Chitnis, vice-president of product at Chhanda Learning Group, a Bengaluru consumer-education firm with three product lines and a growth pod in Lisbon under Lucia Carvalho. “You have told me everything you supervise,” she said. “You have not told me one thing you decided.”

Lokesh did not rewrite his résumé. On 20 April he volunteered six hours a week to an internal product squad working on reconciliation exceptions, and kept it up for 21 weeks — 126 hours. He applied again in July, reached Vaishali’s interview on 4 August and was declined on 11 August. On 14 September, Vriksha Agri Exchange, a two-sided produce marketplace, offered him ₹37 lakh; two days earlier his employer had offered an internal product manager title at ₹48 lakh. He had until 28 September.

2. What the narrative is, and the four schools that disagree

A career-switch narrative is a compressed argument that a person with no track record in a role is nonetheless the right hire for it. Three parts carry it: a pull (why this work), proof (decisions owned, with consequences attached) and a path (why this company, now). Its distinguishing feature is that it must do what a track record normally does, under extreme reading scarcity.

The lineage is older than product management. Michael Spence’s 1973 model of job-market signalling supplies the economics: when ability is unobservable, a signal informs only if it is cheaper for the able to send. Behavioural interviewing followed, in Tom Janz’s patterned behaviour description interview of the early 1980s; the validity literature since — Schmidt and Hunter in 1998, revised downward by Sackett and colleagues in 2022 — still ranks structured interviewing above unstructured. The identity half comes from Dan McAdams’s life-story model and Herminia Ibarra’s transition research, whose 2005 essay with Kent Lineback argued that a change story must make discontinuity cohere.

Out of that lineage four positions have hardened, and practitioners who hold them give flatly contradictory advice.

Table 1. Four schools, and the proposition each would sign
SchoolWould signWould not sign
PositioningThe first read is a seconds-long pattern match on title; the problem is legibility, solved in the writing.That writing substitutes for judgement in the room.
Evidence-firstNothing counts until a product decision has been owned somewhere, including at the present employer.That anyone with no owned decision should apply.
StructuralPick the market where your origin is the credential; most failures are mis-specified lists.That one story travels across archetypes.
IdentityThe story’s first audience is the teller; coherence lets a person behave like a product manager first.That coherence is evidence.

The disagreement is not stylistic: it sends scarce hours to rewriting, to a detour that may cost a year, to research, to reflection. Section 10 asks what would make each wrong.

3. Mechanics: what thirty-four seconds buys

Chhanda opened two product requisitions on 1 July 2026 and closed them on 30 September, a 91-day window. Of 1,240 applications, 868 — 70.0 per cent — came from candidates who had never held a product title and 372 from those who had.

A pivot is 3.5 times less likely to survive the résumé screen (7.1 against 25.0 per cent) and weaker at the manager call (29.0 against 45.2). But both cohorts convert identically at the loop, 33.3 per cent, and pivots convert better at the offer: 1 of 6 against 1 of 14. The loop is not where pivots lose. The screen is.

Now price the stages. Vaishali’s recruiters logged a median of 34 seconds per résumé, 20 minutes per recruiter call and 30 minutes per manager call; each loop ran four interviewers for an hour, with a 45-minute debrief.

Eighty-seven and a half per cent of candidates (1,085 of 1,240) are eliminated inside 6.2 per cent of the selection hours; for pivots alone it is 92.9 per cent, 806 of 868. That judgement takes about half a minute, by a reader whose cheapest cue is the most recent job title. The two hires cost 94.2 hours each. Pivot narratives are written as arguments and read as patterns.

Expert practice follows in seven steps, the first two usually left implicit. Fix the target reading: the sentence you want written in the debrief. Fix the archetype list before writing a word. Do the archaeology: find in specs, tickets and mail threads the places where you decided rather than attended. Attach a consequence with a number and a date. Compress to the 34-second surface — title line, top bullet, one-line summary. Build one openable artefact. Rehearse the spoken form.

Three second-order effects are rarely discussed. The compression that makes you legible narrows you: Charulata became, by design, “the manufacturing person”. The pay you accept to buy entry anchors your next two offers, not just this one. And a referral substitutes for the narrative, so polish can be bought more cheaply with an introduction.

4. The conditions, as testable claims

Four testable claims decide whether the narrative is the right object of effort, and each resolves differently for the two protagonists.

Table 4. Four conditions, applied
ClaimTestCharulataLokesh
The screen, not the loop, bindsScreen rate under 10 per cent, loop untestedTrue: 4.3 per cent over 46 applicationsFalse by August: screened in, lost later
Your origin is a credential somewhereEight or more firms selling to your employer’s customersTrue: 14 manufacturing-software firmsWeak: 5 trade-finance firms
You can name one decision with a numberA decision, a rejected alternative, a figure that movedTrue: the calibration flowFalse in February, true by September
Any pay cut is affordableCumulative gap, not year oneNo cut: ₹24 lakh to ₹29 lakh₹9 lakh in year one, ₹13.5 lakh cumulative

Where the idea misleads is worth stating. In an internal move a sponsor who knows your work matters far more, and a polished story only sounds odd. Where the founder reads every application the 34-second constraint does not bind, and the effort belongs in the artefact. In large organisations with hard grade rules, no narrative clears a structural ineligibility.

5. Edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product firms fracture the narrative. Chhanda runs three lines, and Lucia Carvalho’s growth pod in Lisbon weights activation where the schools line weights institutional selling: the same résumé reads differently by which manager the recruiter routes it to, a routing the candidate cannot see. Two-sided businesses force a choice candidates fudge: Vriksha’s supply side is field operations under another name, so Lokesh’s exception work is a credential there — if he names the side. In regulated products, such as the health cover Chhatra Insurance Services sells under IRDAI filings, an operations origin reads strongly and the risk inverts: hired for constraint management, then judged on product sense nobody asked for. Chakshu runs 14-week firmware cycles, so a story assuming weekly deployment signals a misread business. At Chhavi AI Labs, Vikram Chhabria reads all 300-odd applications himself, looking for anyone who has shipped with an evaluation harness attached.

The seams matter more than the archetypes: recruiters optimise for the manager’s stated criteria, always narrower than the real ones. The sharpest is the referral channel.

Table 5. Screen pass rate by channel, same 1,240 applications

Referrals were 7.7 per cent of applications and 24.5 per cent of screens, a pass rate 3.9 times the direct channel’s. The blended 12.5 per cent is not the average of 39.6 and 10.2; it is 155 divided by 1,240 — which is why channel mix explains more than prose quality.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

Vaishali scored the 62 pivots who passed her screen against 62 of the 806 who did not, on five signals. The columns do not sum: signals co-occur.

Table 6. Five signals, 62 who passed against 62 who did not
SignalPassedDid notLift
Names a decision they owned54 (87.1%)11 (17.7%)4.9×
A number attached to that decision48 (77.4%)9 (14.5%)5.3×
Evidence they chose the problem31 (50.0%)6 (9.7%)5.2×
An artefact a reader can open26 (41.9%)4 (6.5%)6.5×
Motive visible before the search began19 (30.6%)7 (11.3%)2.7×

Note: each column counts candidates showing that signal, so the columns do not sum; one candidate may show several.

The screen is a title match, not a story read. The tell is a candidate who has rewritten the summary paragraph and left the job-title line untouched. The obvious reading, that a better paragraph helps, is wrong: it sits below the fold of a 34-second read.

“Why product?” is the weakest of the five signals. At 2.7× it carries less than half the lift of an openable artefact. Motive is cheap to assert, so it holds little information; experts ask it as a coherence check, not as evidence.

The pivot’s real liability is decision latency, not domain ignorance. Domain knowledge arrives in weeks. The tell is the case round, where the candidate asks for more data three times before committing; panels read that as the old job’s reflex, the commonest reason a well-narrated pivot fails.

Panels are not biased against pivots; screens are. Chhanda’s loop converted both cohorts at 33.3 per cent and offered pivots at 16.7 against 7.1 per cent. A candidate who reaches a loop and then complains of bias is usually misreading a craft failure.

An artefact beats an anecdote, but only if it opens in one click and is small. The 6.5× lift belongs to things actually opened. A twelve-page attachment is not an artefact; it is a second résumé nobody reads.

Volunteering a pay cut costs twice. It surrenders the anchor and signals low confidence in the evidence just presented. The expert states a band with a reason, and lets the recruiter name the first number.

Internal detours buy evidence fast and title slowly. Lokesh’s 126 hours produced a real decision and a real number in 21 weeks, as no weekend project would have. What they did not produce was the right to say “I was the product manager”.

Every origin has a default suspicion, and the first sentence must spend itself on it. Operations is suspected of process without product; engineering of building what is asked; banking of optimising inside a frame someone else set. One story for all three disconfirms none of them.

7. How it changes by product type and company stage

Across product types the differences are real but smaller than commonly claimed. Consumer products want a funnel number; business software wants evidence of handling a buyer and a user who are different people, where an operations manager’s stakeholder history is genuinely relevant, not merely transferable; marketplaces want you to name a side. AI products are the one archetype where the bar has moved in two years: evaluation discipline now reads as core craft, and a candidate from any origin who has built an eval set holds something scarce.

Stage is the stronger variable, and Chirag’s placement book for 2025-26 quantifies it.

Table 7. Lagan Talent Services, 54 product placements, 2025-26
StagePlacementsPivotsPivot share
Seed to Series A12758.3%

Listed or large private8112.5%
Total / blended541731.5%

The blended share is 17 of 54, or 31.5 per cent — not the mean of the four row rates, which is 30.6 per cent, a distinction that matters whenever someone quotes one headline number. The slope is monotonic, from 58.3 per cent at the earliest stage to 12.5 per cent among listed and large private firms, because process substitutes for breadth as a company grows and the screen becomes more title-bound. The implication: spend early effort where the reader is the founder, and treat large-company applications as the channel where only a referral works.

8. Three worked searches

Charulata’s search splits into two phases. In the 56 days from 6 April to 1 June she sent 46 applications — 6 manufacturing software, 19 consumer, 21 horizontal business software — at roughly 0.6 hours each, 27.6 hours in all, for 2 screens. In the 67 days from 1 June to 7 August she sent 21, split 13, 3 and 5 across the same archetypes, at 3.2 hours each, 67.2 hours, plus 38 hours building the one artefact she attached: 105.2 hours. She got 9 screens — 7 from the 13 manufacturing applications, none from the 3 consumer, 2 from the 5 horizontal — three loops, and the offer from Lochan Factory Works, a Pune manufacturing-execution software firm under Lavina Chitale.

The two windows are not the same length — 56 days against 67 — so the comparison has to be per application rather than per day, and nothing below is a rate per week: 2 of 46 is 4.3 per cent, 9 of 21 is 42.9 per cent. Had the first rate held, nine screens would have needed 207 applications — 2 of 46 is exactly 1 in 23, and 9 × 23 = 207 — costing 124.2 hours at 0.6 hours each against the 67.2 the targeted applications took: a saving of 57.0 hours, or 45.9 per cent. Two caveats. Two successes in 46 attempts is a thin base, with a plausible range of roughly 1 to 15 per cent. And she changed both the story and the target list, so her data cannot separate the positioning school from the structural one.

Lokesh’s numbers come from the squad, not the search. Vyapaar handled about 11,400 reconciliation exceptions a month, 78 per cent auto-matched, leaving 2,508 for manual work. The redesign he argued for, against a proposal to add two analysts, raised auto-matching to 91 per cent and left 1,026 — a fall of 1,482, or 59.1 per cent. At 7.5 minutes of analyst time each, monthly manual effort fell from 313.5 to 128.25 hours, a saving of 185.25 hours; at a fully loaded ₹520 an hour, ₹96,330 a month or ₹11.56 lakh a year. One decision, one alternative rejected, one number.

The third search is the instructive failure. Chaitanya Lotlikar, 38, a programme manager at a systems-integration firm on ₹41 lakh, built a narrative around a side project and began applying on 5 January 2026. Over 19 weeks to 18 May he sent 34 applications for 12 screens, a rate of 35.3 per cent, then 7 manager calls, 4 loops and no offers. The narrative was excellent and the craft was not: he lost the product-sense round every time. He had 23 credible targets and had burned 4, 17.4 per cent of his addressable market. The recovery was to stop: nothing for 10 weeks, 20 case sessions at two a week, then 11 applications from 27 July, 5 screens, 3 loops, 2 offers, and ₹34 lakh accepted on 9 September — a cut of ₹7 lakh, or 17.1 per cent.

9. Failure modes and what it costs to notice late

Table 9. Four failure modes
ModeEarly signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Polishing a dead archetypeScreen rate under 10 per cent after 25 applicationsWhich targets sell to my customers?46 applications, 27.6 hours, 56 days
Narrative without craftHigh screen rate, zero loop conversionWhat did I decide when data was missing?19 weeks, 4 of 23 targets burned

One story for all archetypesThe closing sentence survives a name swapWould it be false at the next firm?The whole targeted phase mis-specified

The early signs are cheap and almost nobody collects them. A candidate tracking screen rate per archetype and loop conversion can separate a positioning failure from a craft failure within about 25 applications. Without them the only feedback is silence, which fits every diagnosis.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The positioning school rests on Table 2: when 92.9 per cent of pivots die in 34 seconds, the writing is the constraint and effort elsewhere is premature. It would be wrong if screens were already near their ceiling for well-targeted candidates — close to what Charulata’s 42.9 per cent suggests, a number awkward for the school, since it came from changing the list, not the prose.

The evidence-first school rests on the lift column in Table 6, where an owned decision and a number carry 4.9× and 5.3× against motive’s 2.7×, and on Chaitanya’s loops failing with an excellent story in hand. It would be wrong if the relationship ran the other way: if candidates who describe decisions well simply have better jobs to describe.

The structural school rests on the archetype split, 7 of 13 manufacturing applications screened against 0 of 3 consumer ones, and on Chirag’s slope from 58.3 to 12.5 per cent. It would be wrong where domain-adjacent roles are scarce, as for Lokesh with 5 trade-finance firms, and the adjacency that gets you hired can hold you in a narrow market for years.

The identity school rests on other evidence — Ibarra’s research, and the observation that candidates who have not resolved the story negotiate badly and hedge. It would be wrong if confident narration merely followed from holding good evidence.

One question is unsettled: pivots at Chhanda converted at 16.7 per cent of loops against 7.1 per cent. Is the screen too harsh, leaving only unusually strong pivots, or do pivots bring something the titled cohort does not? Twenty loops cannot separate the explanations.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a better résumé. Someone who has internalised it builds the target list first and treats the résumé as the cheapest of four instruments, the others being the referral, the artefact and the owned decision. They instrument the search: by application 25 they know whether the problem is positioning or craft. They allocate the 90 seconds of a spoken answer deliberately — about 15 seconds to the pull, 50 to two proofs, 25 to the path — and abandon the script when the interviewer has granted the premise. And when the evidence changes, as Lokesh’s did, they rewrite the story to fit it.

12. The two decisions

Charulata accepted Lochan Factory Works on 19 August 2026, twelve days after the offer, at ₹29 lakh against her ₹24 lakh, and started on 1 October. The rise of ₹5 lakh is 20.8 per cent, reduced by a Coimbatore-to-Pune rent difference of about ₹18,000 a month, ₹2.16 lakh a year, for a net gain of ₹2.84 lakh, or 11.8 per cent. The pivot cost her nothing in cash — the least transferable part of her case, since she moved from a lower-paying sector into a higher-paying one.

Lokesh chose on 26 September and took Vriksha Agri Exchange at ₹37 lakh over the internal product title at ₹48 lakh. The internal role paid 4.3 per cent more than his current ₹46 lakh; the external one paid ₹9 lakh less, 19.6 per cent, a cumulative cost of roughly ₹13.5 lakh if the gap closes over two years, plus 0.06 per cent of equity in a company last valued at ₹1,450 crore — ₹87 lakh on paper, ₹21.75 lakh a year across four years of vesting, worth nothing until liquid. His reasoning: the internal role reported to the head of operations with a roadmap set by sales — the title without the craft — while Vriksha reported to a head of product and gave him a marketplace’s supply side to own. He was buying what the title is supposed to signal.

Three questions for discussion. First, Charulata changed her story and her target list in the same week; design the search that would have told her which one mattered, and price it in weeks. Second, Chhanda’s screen removes 92.9 per cent of pivots in 34 seconds each, yet pivots who reach the loop convert better — if you were Vaishali, what would you change, and what new error would you accept? Third, at what cumulative figure would Lokesh’s ₹13.5 lakh trade for a reporting line stop being defensible?

13. Going deeper

Transitioning into product management is the parent decision, covering the internal-move and side-project routes used here. PM interviews comes next: the narrative buys the loop, and the loop is decided by product sense, where Chaitanya failed. Building a PM portfolio and narrative develops the artefact with the highest lift in Table 6, 6.5×. Your first 90 days in a PM role is where a pivot’s story is validated or falsified. A PM’s operating system and continuous learning as a PM close the decision-latency gap Section 6 names as the pivot’s liability. Confidence, doubt and judgement is the honest companion to the identity school.
case40v1-craft.pivot.narrative:
Girish Sathaye: Three Sentences and Four Doors

A case on the career-switch narrative, set in Pune and Bengaluru, October 2026

1. The night before

At ten past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Girish Sathaye sat on the floor of the second bedroom of his flat in Wakad, Pune, with a printed page in his hand. On it were three paragraphs, each exactly three sentences long, each a different account of the same ten years of his working life. His laptop showed a calendar invitation: five rounds, from 9.30 a.m. on Tuesday, 13 October, at the Bellandur office of Gantavya Fleet Network, for the post of Product Manager II, Fleet Operations.

Girish was thirty-four. He had spent ten years at Gatiman Industries, a Pune maker of electric two-wheelers, the last three of them running service engineering across 240 franchised dealer workshops. He held a diploma in mechanical engineering from 2013 and a part-time bachelor's degree finished in the evenings in June 2022. He had never written production code, never carried a product title, and never worked anywhere whose revenue came from software.

Three things were true at once. He had a signed offer from Gulmohar Energy Systems, a charging and battery-swap network, worth ₹42 lakh a year, which lapsed on Friday, 16 October — three days after the Gantavya loop and seven days before Gantavya would decide. He had an internal offer from Gargi Nalawade to become Product Manager, Connected Services at Gatiman, which had to be taken before her headcount expired on 31 October. And he had a recruiter in Warsaw, a coach in Mumbai, a boss who did not want to lose him, and a finance controller two floors below him whose note, if an interviewer ever read it, would take apart the one number his best story rested on.

What he had to settle before Tuesday was narrower than any of that: which of the three paragraphs to say in the first four minutes of the first round.

2. Gatiman Industries, and a decision made in 2021

Gatiman was founded in 2014 by two engineers from Pune's components belt. Its first scooter shipped in 2017; by FY26 it was a credible fifth name in Indian electric two-wheelers, behind Ola Electric, TVS, Bajaj and Ather. Its plant was at Chakan; in Baner, some 180 engineers maintained the vehicle firmware, a rider app, a dealer ordering portal and the telemetry pipeline that fed all three.

The decision that constrained Girish's October was taken in 2021, when Gatiman chose to grow its service footprint through franchised workshops rather than company-owned centres. The logic was capital: franchising reached 240 workshops in four years on other people's money. The consequence was organisational. Because the workshops were somebody else's business, their software was classified as channel tooling and owned by Sales Operations, not by Product. Connected Services, Gargi's group, had a roadmap, a director and four product managers, but no engineers of its own; it borrowed from the platform team and from vendors.

So the Console — the diagnostics and warranty-claim tool Girish had conceived, specified and driven into all 240 workshops — was built by four engineers from Gahan Software Works, a Pune vendor, under a statement of work signed by Service. It was also why the role Gargi was offering sat, in the HR system, inside the Service Operations job family. The title would read Product Manager. The job code would not.

3. The industry around the decision

Electric two-wheelers had become an operations business rather than a novelty business. With FAME II closed, PM E-DRIVE subsidies tapering and AIS 156 battery-safety requirements now routine, the competitive question had moved from range to cost per service visit, and warranty expense per vehicle was a number boards asked about. That favoured a man whose decade had been spent inside it, and it was the basis of the Gulmohar offer: swap stations need someone who knows what a battery pack looks like after eighteen months in Pune traffic.

Bengaluru, meanwhile, had hardened its bar. Gantavya sold a fleet-operations platform to last-mile logistics operators, including two that moved parcels for the large quick-commerce and food-delivery platforms, and it hired product managers the way Freshworks, Zoho and Postman did: product sense, metrics, execution, a craft round with design, and a bar-raiser. Domain knowledge was welcome in those rooms but was not what the rounds measured.

And Gatiman was arguing with itself about whether connected services was a product line or a cost centre. The ordering portal existed to capture spare-parts revenue, the telemetry pipeline to serve warranty analytics; neither had a price. The FY28 planning cycle, opening in January 2027, would decide whether Connected Services got engineers of its own.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The pivot began in October 2024, when a dealer in Solapur told him his technicians were guessing at battery faults from a code read off the vehicle display, and that a wrong guess meant a replaced pack, a rejected warranty claim and a ruined month. Girish wrote eleven pages describing what the workshop needed, had a vendor statement of work approved by Ghanshyam Barve, and piloted the Console in twenty workshops. On 1 April 2025 it went live in all 240.

Through FY26, the year from April 2025 to March 2026, warranty cost per serviced vehicle fell from ₹2,000 to ₹1,600, a drop of ₹400, or twenty per cent. By March 2026, 150 of the 240 workshops were opening the Console in a given week, which is 62.5 per cent. Girish was promoted to Senior Manager in April 2026. In May a former colleague told him that what he had been doing since that Solapur conversation was product management, and that he was doing it for a service manager's salary and no stock.

He began applying on 1 June 2026. Over the thirteen weeks to 30 August he sent 180 applications, about fourteen a week, rotating three versions of his story sixty each. Exhibit 1 records what came back; read at the top of the funnel, the builder-led version drew three times the screens of the domain-led one.

Four things he believed in June had become unsafe by October. The first was that the ₹400 saving was his to quote. On 2 September, preparing an internal slide, he found a note by Gitanjali Deshingkar attributing ₹5 crore of the FY26 warranty improvement to a revised charger harness that entered production on 1 July 2025 — three months after the Console went live — and only ₹1 crore to better diagnosis at the workshop. Ghanshyam Barve read the same note and reached the opposite conclusion, for reasons set out in Exhibit 3.

The second was that the screen rate told him what to say in the room. By the end of September his builder-led story had produced three final loops and no offers, while his domain-led story had produced one loop and the only offer he held.

The third was that the Console counted as shipping. In the Gopuram Retail Systems loop on 4 September a product director asked who had written the acceptance tests, who had decided the release sequence, and what he had cut to hit the April date. His answers named Gahan Software Works three times. The rejection, two days later, said he had been the customer of a project rather than the owner of a product.

The fourth was that an internal move was the easy fallback. On 14 September Gargi offered him Connected Services, and he learned that the title he had imagined as a stepping stone was recorded in a job family external recruiters had already learned to discount.

5. The people

Girish Sathaye, thirty-four, Senior Manager, Service Engineering, Pune. He says he wants to own a product rather than a process, and has been doing the work already; he has a home-loan EMI of ₹32,000 a month and no stock in anything. He is not saying that he fears the Bengaluru metrics round more than unemployment, and has twice drafted an email withdrawing from the loop.

Gargi Nalawade, Director, Connected Services, Gatiman, Pune. Her position: the domain is the moat, and no outsider learns 240 workshops in a year. Her incentive is a vacancy she loses on 31 October and a roadmap that needs a franchise owner to answer the phone. She is not saying that the FY28 cycle may fold her group into Sales Operations, nor that she has twice asked HR to recode the role into the product job family and twice been refused.

Ghanshyam Barve, Vice-President, Service and Quality, Girish's manager for three years. He argues that the Console's gains are real and Gitanjali's attribution arithmetically impossible — and on her own numbers he is right. He also has a 90-day notice period he will not waive and a quality-award submission built on the Console. He is not saying that he has told Gargi he would rather Girish stayed in Service, nor that his submission quotes the ₹8 crore figure.

Gitanjali Deshingkar, Finance Controller, Gatiman, Pune. Her note assigns most of the FY26 improvement to the harness revision; her incentive is a cost-share negotiation with the harness supplier, in which a large attributed saving strengthens Gatiman's hand. She is not saying that her ₹5 crore came from allocating the total improvement in proportion to engineering change orders raised in the year, by a method set out in a footnote nobody has questioned.

Gunvant Kanetkar, Vice-President, Product, Gantavya Fleet Network, Bengaluru. He told Girish on 5 October that he was tired of product managers who had never stood in a workshop, and that domain scar tissue was the scarcest thing in his org. His incentive is a Fleet Operations roadmap that slips because nobody on it has run an operation. He is not saying that an internal transfer from customer success is in the same loop, with three years inside the product.

Gurveer Dhaliwal, Head of Data Science, Gantavya, Melbourne. He runs the metrics round at 7 a.m. his time and has failed eleven of the last fifteen candidates: a candidate who quotes a large rupee saving without naming the counterfactual, he says, does not know what evidence is. He is not saying that he switched into product analytics from civil engineering nine years ago and was nearly broken by his own first loop.

Grazyna Majewska, principal consultant, Grisma Talent Partners, working from Warsaw on the firm's India desk. She placed the Gulmohar mandate and says: get the word product onto the CV, and the next move is easy. Her fee is one month of fixed pay, ₹3 lakh on ₹36 lakh fixed, clawed back if he leaves within six months. Her tracker counts 42 recruiter screens where his own counts 36, and she does not think the gap matters.

Gandhali Zunjarrao, former product lead, now a coach in Mumbai, paid ₹40,000 for four sessions. She wrote the three-sentence structure Girish uses and argues for the outcome-led version, because a hiring manager remembers one number. Her incentive is a cohort programme whose marketing rests on outcome-led stories working. She is not saying that her sample of sixty placed clients is almost entirely MBAs leaving consulting and banking, not diploma engineers leaving service.

Gitesh Talegaonkar, a former Gatiman colleague, now a product manager at a Bengaluru SaaS company and in Ho Chi Minh City for the quarter. He made the same switch in 2023 by taking a product analyst role two levels down and a pay cut, reaching product manager in twenty months, and tells Girish that Path D is the honest route. He is not saying that his wife's income carried the household through the cut.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is Girish's own tracker. The rotation was disciplined: sixty applications on each version, interleaved weekly, so no version got the easier months. Read down the screen-rate column, the builder-led version is three times the domain-led one; read across to the right, it is the domain-led version that produced the only offer. Grazyna and Gandhali have both read this table and drawn opposite conclusions from it.

Exhibit 3 is the number his best story rests on, with the disagreement beside it. The arithmetic can be done in the margin, and two senior people at Gatiman have done it and disagree.

Exhibit 4 sets out the money. The columns are not comparable: Gulmohar is signed paper, Gantavya's two columns are verbally quoted bands, and Path D has never been offered to anyone. Girish had noticed, and found it uncomfortable, that the analyst path pays exactly what he earns today.

7. Voices

Gandhali Zunjarrao, email, 3 October:

Lead with the eight crore. Nobody argues with a rupee figure in the first four minutes, and your problem is not credibility, it is memorability. The Console is a story about a vendor. The crore is a story about you.

Gurveer Dhaliwal, in a Gantavya interviewer calibration thread, 29 September, shown to Girish by nobody:

Please stop passing candidates who recite a savings number. Ask them what would have happened without them. If the answer is a shrug, that is the answer.

Ghanshyam Barve, on a call, 4 October, as Girish noted it afterwards:

Her note cannot be right. The harness went into production in July; three-quarters of the vehicles we serviced last year never had it. Quote the saving outside this building if you must, but do not let anyone show you her footnote first.

Gargi Nalawade, in a meeting room in Baner, 14 September:

You are the only person here who can call a dealer in Solapur at nine at night and get an honest answer. In Bengaluru that is a line on a CV. Here it is the product.

Gunvant Kanetkar, closing the screening call, 5 October:

Do not tell me you have always been a product manager without knowing it. Tell me what you got wrong in the workshop rollout and what it cost. Then I will believe the rest.

Gitesh Talegaonkar, voice note from Ho Chi Minh City, 8 October:

You are asking which of four doors to walk through. The question is who signs off your work for the next two years, because that is the only thing that will be on the page the next time you do this.

8. The options as Girish sees them

Path A: the internal move. Accept Gargi's role before 31 October. ₹34 lakh, no relocation, no notice period, and a roadmap where his ten years are an asset rather than an anomaly. Against it: no engineers of his own, a job code in Service Operations, and a January planning cycle that may remove the roadmap. In eighteen months he could say he had been a product manager; he is not sure he could say what he had shipped.

Path B: Gulmohar Energy Systems. Signed paper at ₹42 lakh, a swap network that needs what he knows, and Grazyna's argument that the word product compounds. Against it: the role reports to Operations, the company has eleven software engineers in all, and the thing he would own is a network rather than a product. Taking it means accepting before Tuesday, or declining a loop he spent four months earning.

Path C: Gantavya at PM II. The real thing: ₹44 lakh, ₹8 lakh a year of equity, a product org that behaves like one, and Gunvant's appetite for domain scar tissue. Against it: a metrics round that has failed eleven of its last fifteen candidates, an internal candidate with three years inside the product, Bengaluru, and a decision seven days after his only offer lapses.

Path D: the step down. Ask Gantavya to consider him as a product analyst at ₹30 lakh and climb, as Gitesh did. Against it: nobody has offered it, it means asking Gunvant to lower his own requisition, and it converts a ten-year career into an entry-level one in a sentence.

Girish had drawn these four as Figure 1 and been satisfied with it until Gitesh's voice note. The axes were how much software the product had and how much his domain was worth. Neither was the thing that had decided every outcome in Exhibit 1, which was what he said in the first four minutes and whether the next forty could be spent testing it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Gulmohar offer lapses at the end of Friday, 16 October; Grazyna says an extension is possible but has not asked, and asking signals the existence of Gantavya. The Gantavya loop is five rounds on Tuesday, 13 October, with a decision promised by Friday, 23 October, ten days later. Gargi's headcount dies on 31 October.

Gatiman's notice period is 90 days and Ghanshyam will not waive it. Gulmohar wants a joining date of 1 December, which means serving about 45 days and buying out the other 45 at fixed salary — ₹3.25 lakh from his own pocket, against an EMI of ₹32,000 a month and no stock to sell. Policy allows no early release in the quarter before the annual quality awards, for which Ghanshyam has entered the Console, quoting the ₹8 crore. If Girish uses that figure in a Bengaluru interview room and the room asks for the finance note, he will be describing, under his own name, a number his employer's controller has attributed elsewhere.

At half past midnight on Monday, 12 October, he laid the three paragraphs side by side on the floor. Version A had produced the only offer and did not mention a product. Version B had opened three times as many doors and closed none of them, and its first sentence named a vendor's work as his own. Version C led with a crore figure two of his own colleagues could not agree on, and that the hardest interviewer in Bengaluru had told his panel to distrust. Somewhere in the building a scooter alarm went off and stopped. He had thirty-three hours before the first round, and no fourth paragraph.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1 as Grazyna reads it, then as Gandhali reads it. What must each assume about the funnel for their conclusion to hold, and which assumption is easier to test with 180 applications?
  2. Write the three sentences you would have Girish say in the first four minutes on Tuesday. Mark which claims an interviewer can test inside forty minutes and which can only be asserted.
  3. Exhibit 3 contains two arithmetically honest quantities, ₹8 crore and ₹4 crore, and one attribution that does not survive its own numbers. What, precisely, is Girish entitled to claim about the Console, and in whose terms?
  4. Gurveer wants the counterfactual, and the split he asks for has never been produced. What should a candidate do with a number they believe but cannot defend?
  5. Using Exhibit 4 and section 9, price each path in cash, in optionality and in the evidence it will generate by 2028. Does the ₹14 lakh gap between Path D and Path C measure what Girish thinks it measures?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October. What should Girish do before the loop, what should he say to Gargi, Grazyna and Ghanshyam, and if Gatiman's management committee asked him on Wednesday why he was leaving a function he had helped build, what exactly should he answer?
case20v1-craft.pivot.narrative:
Bindu Menon and the Two Stories

A case on constructing the career-switch narrative

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Bindu Menon sat at her dining table in Powai, Mumbai, with two documents open on her laptop. One was an offer letter from Bunkar Industries, a Nashik-based engineering and distribution group, for the post of Manager, Product Strategy. It expired on Wednesday, 14 October. The other was a calendar invitation for a four-round interview loop at Bharosa Works, a Pune start-up, for a product manager role. The loop was on Friday, 16 October, two days after the offer lapsed.

Bindu was twenty-nine, an engagement manager at Bodhan Partners, a Mumbai consulting firm of about ninety consultants, where she had spent six years after an engineering degree and an MBA. She wanted to become a product manager. She now had to decide which story to carry into the Bharosa loop, and whether to take the safe offer before she knew the result.

2. Company background

Bharosa Works was founded in 2018 in Pune. Its app lets kirana stores order stock from distributors and, increasingly, buy on short-term credit extended by partner lenders under the RBI's digital lending rules. Retailers pay through UPI, settled over NPCI rails. Bharosa competes for the same shopkeeper's attention with Udaan and Jumbotail, with Flipkart's wholesale arm and with Reliance Retail's JioMart partner programme. It had about 600 employees and had just raised a growth round for its credit product.

Bunkar Industries was older and steadier: a family-promoted group making agricultural implements and distributing them through dealers across Maharashtra and Gujarat. Its new product strategy team was meant to digitise dealer ordering. It was not clear who would build anything.

3. The situation

Bindu's consulting work had been good, and one project stood out. For a lender client, she had spent five months with a Pune engineering team building a loan-status assistant for field agents. She had written the requirements, run weekly demos, and argued the team out of a feature nobody needed. Of 400 field agents, 120 used it weekly within a quarter.

Her first draft of the switch story, written in July, read as follows.

I have spent six years solving structural problems for banks. I enjoy strategy but want to own outcomes. Product management is where strategy gets executed.

She called it Version A. Between 1 July and 26 August, a period of eight weeks, she sent twenty applications with Version A and twenty with a second draft, Version B, alternating them week by week. Version B was built around the loan assistant.

Last year I led a team of five engineers to ship a loan-status assistant that 120 of 400 field agents now use every week. I realised I enjoyed the shipping more than the slide that justified it. I want to do that full time, on a product where the user is a shopkeeper rather than a bank.

Exhibit 1 shows the results. Version B opened more doors at the first stage, thirty per cent against twenty. Each version produced exactly one final loop, but the Version A loop was Bunkar's strategy role, which carries no product title, while the Version B loop was Bharosa's product manager role. Bindu knew the sample was tiny. Recruiters who read Version A asked about frameworks; those who read Version B asked about trade-offs.

Exhibit 2 places the key dates side by side. The Bunkar offer had arrived on Thursday, 1 October, after a final loop on 28 September. Bunkar's HR head had hinted that an extension was possible but unlikely beyond Tuesday, 20 October.

The global view was mixed. Bela Mathur, Bharosa's design lead in Lisbon, would sit on Bindu's panel and was known to distrust polished candidates. A data lead in Melbourne ran the metrics round and, Bindu had been told, asked every candidate to critique a number rather than recite one.

4. The people

Bhuvan Sethi, Head of Product at Bharosa Works in Pune, was hiring two product managers. He had told Bindu on a call that he wanted evidence of shipping with engineers, and that he had hired two ex-consultants who were later excellent and one who left in eight months, always for the same reason: the story had been about the resume, not the work.

Balram Kulkarni, in Bengaluru, was Bindu's mentor, an engineer turned product lead at a fintech. He thought Bunkar was a trap: a strategy title tends to stay a strategy title, and he had seen colleagues spend three years trying to get out of the box that a safe offer built.

Bimla Rastogi, partner at Bodhan Partners in Mumbai, wanted Bindu to stay. She had hinted at a promotion to principal, with a rise that Bindu estimated at ₹8 lakh.

5. Compensation

Exhibit 3 compares the options in annual terms. Bindu's current package was ₹38 lakh fixed and ₹6 lakh variable. Bharosa had indicated that her profile fit the product manager level, PM2, but that a senior product manager level was possible only if she could demonstrate two shipped products. Its equity is a four-year grant, shown here as one quarter per year. Bunkar offers no equity.

Exhibit 3 shows that the Bunkar offer paid ₹2 lakh more than the likely Bharosa package, but contained no equity. The senior role would pay ₹12 lakh more than Bunkar and ₹20 lakh more than Bindu's current package, but was the least likely outcome. In her own estimate, the real question was not which number was largest but which story she could defend in front of four sceptical interviewers.

6. The options

Option 1: accept Bunkar now. The offer is certain and pays ₹8 lakh more than today. The upside is a title on her resume that includes the word product, and a base from which to move later. The cost is that Balram's warning may prove right, the role may involve little building, and she would have to cancel the Bharosa loop or take it with an offer already signed.

Option 2: go to Bharosa with Version A, aimed at the senior role. It shows ambition and plays to her proven strength in structured thinking, and the senior package is worth ₹64 lakh. The cost is that Bhuvan has said plainly that he wants evidence of shipping, and a strategy-led story aimed above her level invites exactly the doubts Bela will test. The Bunkar offer would lapse during the wait.

Option 3: go to Bharosa with Version B, aimed at PM2, and ask Bunkar for an extension to 20 October. The story rests on an evidenced product experience, and the role is a real product job. The cost is a ₹2 lakh lower package than Bunkar, the risk of rejection, and the real possibility that Bunkar refuses and the offer lapses with nothing in hand on 14 October.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1 critically. What can Bindu conclude from forty applications, and what can she not?
  2. Compare Versions A and B sentence by sentence. Which claims can an interviewer test, and which can only be asserted?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, what does Bindu give up in cash, and what does she gain, by choosing each path? How should she value equity that may be worth nothing?
  4. Which option would you take, and what would you tell Bimla, Balram and Bunkar's HR head?

8. A note for the learner

The career-switch narrative answers one question: why should we believe you will do this job? A good story has three sentences. The first offers proof of product work you have already done, with a number. The second names what that work taught you about what you want. The third connects that wish to this company's actual problem. Version B follows this shape; Version A has a destination but no proof.

The defensible path is Option 3. The evidence in Exhibit 1 is thin, but the direction is consistent with what Bhuvan said and with what recruiters asked, and the mechanism is plausible: an interviewer can probe a shipped assistant for forty minutes, but cannot probe the sentence that strategy gets executed. Aiming at PM2 rather than the senior role avoids asking the panel to overlook her gap, and the ₹6 lakh total rise over her current package is entirely equity: fixed plus variable is ₹44 lakh, exactly what she earns today, so the cash rise is nil and the package sits ₹2 lakh below Bunkar's ₹52 lakh. She would be paid in paper, not salary, for the move she wants. An extension request costs little, provided she tells Bunkar why.

If Bunkar refuses, she should still decline on 14 October, because a strategy title is a different career and a signed offer would weaken her answer to Bela. If Bharosa then rejects her, she keeps her job and her story, and tests it again. Option 1 is rational for a candidate who needs the money more than the move, but Bindu has said she does not.
exp20v2-craft.pivot.narrative:
The career-switch narrative

How a consultant, engineer or banker explains the move into product in a way that lands.

1. Opening: twelve weeks and an eight-lakh question

On 12 January 2026, Sumedha Wadkar, a 29-year-old engagement manager at a Mumbai strategy consultancy, sat down with a spreadsheet and a decision. She earned ₹38 lakh a year and had spent five years on banking and lending engagements. She wanted to become a product manager. A friend who had made the same move had given her a plan: send 150 applications in twelve weeks and let volume do the work. Against that, she had one real lead. Tanvi Wakankar, head of product at Tijori Systems, a Pune merchant-payments firm of about 340 people, was hiring one associate product manager and had agreed to a call.

The stakes were concrete. Tijori’s likely offer was ₹30 lakh, which is ₹8 lakh below her current pay, a cut of 21 per cent (8 divided by 38). A cut of that size is worth taking only if the move succeeds, and it fails quietly: a candidate whose résumé is read as “consultant” is screened out within seconds, and never learns why. Her first three applications in December had produced silence. Her résumé was accurate but lacked a narrative.

Her first call with Tanvi was set for 9 February, 28 days away. If it went well, a final round would follow, and Tijori wanted an answer from any selected candidate within a fortnight of it.

2. The idea

A career-switch narrative is a short, structured account of why a person who has done one kind of work is now the right hire for another. It is not a biography, and it is not a list of transferable skills. It answers three questions a hiring manager is silently asking: why do you want this, what evidence shows you can do it, and why here? A switcher has no track record in the role, so the story substitutes for it.

No single person invented it. It descends from behavioural interviewing, developed by industrial psychologists in the 1970s and 1980s on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour. Its familiar form is Situation, Task, Action, Result, usually shortened to STAR. The switch narrative applies that logic to an entire career instead of one anecdote. The three-part structure used on this page, pull, proof, path, is a practitioner convention and not a published framework, so treat it as a working tool.

The sentence Sumedha could repeat without sounding glib: “I have spent five years finding out what customers need and recommending what to build, and I now want to be the person who builds it and answers for the result.”

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the first two are the ones practitioners leave implicit. Step one is to choose the target reading: the single sentence you want a manager to write in the debrief. For Sumedha, it was “a consultant who has already behaved like a product person.”

Step two is to translate the vocabulary. A consultant “recommends”; a product manager “decides” and lives with it. An engineer “implements”; a product manager chooses what to implement. A banker “structures a deal”; a product manager runs a flow that thousands of users pass through. Only the verb and the owner of the decision change.

Step three is to audit the evidence, scoring each résumé claim for whether it shows ownership, contact with customers, and a measured outcome. Step four is to rewrite or cut the claims that score low. Step five is to rehearse the spoken form at about ninety seconds, so that the story survives the first five minutes of an interview, when most candidates are judged. The worked example below performs step three and step four on Sumedha’s actual résumé.

4. A worked example

Sumedha scored six résumé bullets on three axes, each from 0 to 3: Ownership (did she decide, or only advise?), Customer contact (did she observe real users?), and Measured outcome (did a number change?). The maximum per bullet is 9, and across six bullets 54.

Table 1. First pass: résumé as written (scores 0 to 3 per axis)
BulletOCMBullet total
1. Built a market-sizing model for a lender1012
2. Interviewed 22 customers of a lender’s mobile app1203
3. Recommended cutting KYC (identity-verification) steps from 9 to 62114
4. Ran weekly steering meetings with the CFO1001
5. Wrote a 60-slide final deck0000
6. Prototyped a loan-status tracker with 2 engineers; tested with 31 users3216
Total85316

The total is 16 of a possible 54, or 29.6 per cent. The column totals expose the pattern: ownership collects 8 points, customer contact 5, and measured outcomes only 3. She had been rewarded for advising and analysing, and her résumé showed it. Bullet 6 was the only one that read as product work, and it sat last, where a reader skimming for ten seconds would not reach it.

Now change one input. She went back to the engagement files and found what bullet 3 had left out: she had watched the 22 customers from bullet 2 abandon the form at the document-upload step, and the bank had adopted her cut. KYC completion rose from 61 to 74 per cent, a gain of 13 percentage points. Rewritten as “Decided, after watching 22 users abandon the upload step, to cut KYC from 9 steps to 6; completion rose from 61 to 74 per cent,” the bullet scores O 3, C 2, M 2, a total of 7 instead of 4.

The grand total becomes 16 + 3 = 19, which is 35.2 per cent of 54. The larger effect comes from selection. Cutting bullets 4 and 5, which scored 1 and 0, leaves four bullets (1, 2, 3 and 6) scoring 2, 3, 7 and 6, which is 18 of a possible 36, or 50 per cent. Before the rewrite and the cut, those same four bullets scored 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15 of 36, or 41.7 per cent. One rewrite and a cut moved the résumé’s evidence density from about 30 per cent to 50 per cent without a single new fact.

Targeting then multiplied the effect. Sumedha compared two twelve-week strategies as expected values, using conversion rates she had gathered from three friends who had switched.

Table 2. Two twelve-week strategies, expected values
StepA: generic, volumeB: targeted narrative
Applications15040
Screen rate8%30%
Screening calls (applications × screen rate)1212
Interview rate after screen50%50%
Interviews66
Offer rate per interview1 in 6 (16.7%)1 in 3 (33.3%)
Offers12
Hours per application0.52.5
Hours spent (applications × hours each)75100
Hours per offer (total hours ÷ offers)7550

Strategy B costs more total hours, 100 against 75, but produces twice the offers, so it costs 50 hours per offer against 75. Change one input: if tailoring takes 3.5 hours per application instead of 2.5, total hours become 140 and the cost per offer 70, which still beats 75. The break-even is 3.75 hours per application (40 × 3.75 = 150, divided by 2 offers, equals 75). The arithmetic shows that targeting wins as long as it stays under 3.75 hours per application. It does not show that her rates are right, which is why they are the first thing to test.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A narrative is not a cover story

The story is built from true episodes selected and framed; it is never invented. Interviewers probe the third question after any claim, and a story that cannot survive “what exactly did you decide?” collapses on the spot. Selection is legitimate. Embellishment is fatal.

Transferable skills are not proof

“Strong analytical and stakeholder skills” is a claim. It distinguishes no one. Proof is a decision, a date and a number, as in the KYC bullet.

The target reading depends on the origin

A consultant must disprove “advises but does not ship.” An engineer, such as Sahil Tawde, who moved from backend development, must disprove “builds what is asked and has not questioned why.” A banker must disprove “works only inside process.” The same facts need different framing for each origin.

Pull is not passion

“I am passionate about products” says nothing checkable. A pull points at behaviour already visible: “I kept rebuilding the status tracker on weekends.” Behaviour before the switch is the best evidence of intent.

The story cannot answer for the role’s demands

A strong narrative gets you into the interview. It does not prove you can prioritise a backlog or read a funnel. Candidates who rely on it alone often stall at the case round.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early-stage and large

In consumer products, the proof that lands is usage evidence: retention, activation, a funnel step you moved. In B2B products, buyers and users are different people, so proof of working with two audiences, for example the CFO who pays and the operations clerk who clicks, reads as an advantage, and a consultant’s stakeholder experience becomes genuinely relevant. In marketplaces, which must keep supply and demand balanced, a narrative that mentions both sides, such as lenders and borrowers, signals the right instinct.

Company size shifts the weighting. At an early-stage firm of fifty people, the manager is buying breadth and speed, so the path section (“why here, why now”) and evidence of working without process matter most. At a large firm such as Flipkart or a major bank’s digital unit, the manager is buying judgement inside structure, and the proof section about stakeholders and outcome measurement carries more weight.

7. Common mistakes

Reciting the résumé chronologically

Symptom: the interviewer interrupts at minute four with “so why product?” Misunderstanding: the candidate treats the story as history rather than an argument. Diagnostic: time the first answer; if the pull is not stated within the first 20 seconds, restructure.

Apologising for the origin

Symptom: phrases such as “I know I do not have a PM background, but…” Misunderstanding: the origin is treated as a deficit instead of evidence. Diagnostic: record a mock answer and count the hedges; none should precede a claim.

Unscored claims

Symptom: peers cannot repeat your proof back after hearing it once. Misunderstanding: the proof has no number or owner. Diagnostic: run Table 1 on your own bullets and rewrite any scoring under 4 of 9.

One story for every employer

Symptom: a high application count and a low screen rate, as in strategy A. Misunderstanding: the path section was never customised. Diagnostic: ask whether the final sentence would still make sense if the company name were swapped.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Sumedha’s opening to Tanvi on 9 February runs about ninety seconds. The pull comes first: she had spent a year watching lending customers abandon a form and wanted to be the one who fixed it. The proof follows with two episodes, the KYC cut and the loan-status tracker, each with a decision, a user count and a number. The path closes it: Tijori’s merchants face the same drop-off at onboarding, and an associate role would let her work on it from the first week.

Every sentence can be checked, and the closing sentence could not be said to any other employer.

9. Closing

Sumedha chose targeting over volume. The reasoning was the arithmetic in Table 2: at 50 hours per offer against 75, with a break-even of 3.75 hours per application that she could stay under. She rewrote her weakest bullets, cut two, and sent 40 tailored applications, with Tijori first. Her final round with Tanvi took place on 3 March, 22 days after the first call, and Tijori made its offer at ₹30 lakh with a deadline of 13 March. She accepted on 12 March, judging the ₹8 lakh gap worth paying because the story had now been tested.

To go further, learn how interviewers score product-sense and case questions, because the narrative earns the interview and these decide it. Read next about transitioning into product management more broadly, where this story sits inside a larger plan involving internal moves, side projects and role choice.

Two questions to sit with. First, take your last three résumé bullets and score them on ownership, customer contact and outcome: which one would you keep if you could keep only one, and what does that tell you about your pull? Second, if your conversion rates were half of Sumedha’s, would targeting still win on hours per offer, and what would you do with the hours it saved?
case40v1-craft.interview.frameworks.trap:
The Scorecard and the Rambler: Nishchay Insurance Works Hires a Renewals PM

A case on hiring judgement and what a framework actually proves. Sunday, 18 October 2026, Mumbai.

1. The night before

The rain had stopped over Lower Parel by nine, and Nilanjana Sheth had the twelfth floor of the Nishchay Insurance Works office almost to herself. On the table were three closed scorecards, a printed take-home exercise with a figure circled twice in pencil, and a note from her talent lead she had read four times without deciding.

By Monday morning, 19 October 2026, she had to name the person who would own renewals and persistency on Nishchay's agent app. One candidate had scored 4.4 out of 5 on the company's interview rubric and was, the panel agreed, the most polished product thinker they had met all year. Another had scored 3.4, below the offer threshold of 3.8, and had spent forty minutes of a sixty-minute round circling a problem without once announcing what he was doing. A third already worked for the company.

The complication was the exercise. The polished candidate had put a number on the page that could not be true, had been invited to revisit it, and had restated it. The rambler, whose note had looked two days late and had in fact sat in the spam quarantine since the deadline, had the number very nearly right and could not explain how without going back to the beginning.

Nishtha Rajadhyaksha's competing offer from a Bengaluru lender expired at 5 p.m. on Wednesday, 21 October. Dussehra was on Tuesday; half her panel would be unreachable.

2. Nishchay Insurance Works, and a decision made in 2024

Nishchay Insurance Works was founded in Mumbai in 2017 by Xerxes Doctor, a former bancassurance head, to sell small-ticket health and accident cover in tier-2 and tier-3 India. Its product was not the policy — partner insurers underwrote those — but the agent: a Marathi, Hindi, Kannada and Telugu app through which some 41,000 part-time agents, most running a shop or a tuition class alongside, sold and serviced cover averaging ₹1,480 of annual premium. By October 2026 the app carried 21.0 lakh policies in force, an annualised book of ₹310.8 crore, of which 6.3 lakh of the 21.0 lakh policies fell due in the October to December quarter, 30 per cent of the book. Persistency was the one number the board watched, and it had been drifting.

The decision that shaped Nilanjana's Sunday had been taken two years earlier. In 2024 a product manager hired for the claims module shipped a nominee-change flow that did not retain the audit trail the partner insurer's compliance team required. The feature was pulled in eleven days; the embarrassment lasted longer. Xerxes concluded that Nishchay interviewed on charm, and bought a structured interviewing programme from a Pune consultancy at ₹18 lakh a year, licensed through March 2028. Panels now scored five dimensions, each out of five. One was Structure: "applies a recognised product framework and signposts its steps". Offers required an average of 3.8.

On 15 October, looking for ammunition, Nilanjana re-read the 2024 post-mortem. The failed hire had not lacked structure: he had run a clean discovery process and never asked whether a rule existed. The rubric bought in response did not test for that, and still did not.

3. The industry

Nishchay sat in a crowded, heavily regulated market. Policybazaar dominated digital comparison; Acko and Go Digit had built direct brands; LIC and Star Health commanded trust in exactly the towns Nishchay's agents worked; PhonePe and Paytm had made insurance a tab inside apps households opened daily. The IRDAI's Bima Sugam exchange promised to make distribution a thinner business, and the ambition of insurance for all by 2047 had pulled every large balance sheet towards the same small-ticket customer.

Two regulatory facts bore on the open role. The thirty-day grace period means a policy not renewed on its due date is not lapsed, so a dashboard counting due-date misses as lapses overstates the problem by weeks. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act constrained what Nishchay could do with policyholder data and, the talent lead kept pointing out, candidate data.

Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Amsterdam, customer success in Nairobi, where a Kenyan microinsurance pilot was Nishchay's only overseas revenue, and partnerships in Lisbon. A panel loop therefore took eleven working days, and no two interviewers met a candidate in the same room.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The requisition for Product Manager, Renewals and Persistency opened on 7 August 2026; Exhibit 4 shows the funnel from 1,240 applications to three finalists. Nishtha Rajadhyaksha, 29, a product manager at a large Bengaluru lending platform, had been coached visibly and expensively. Xavier Noronha, 33, had come up through claims operations at a third-party administrator in Margao before four years as a product analyst at a Kochi insurer; he had no MBA and no vocabulary for what he did. Nitya Samant, 26, had spent three years on Nishchay's support desk in Pune.

The panel met on Wednesday, 14 October. Exhibit 1 carries the scorecards: Nishtha averaged 4.4, Xavier 3.4, Nitya 3.2. Only Nishtha cleared 3.8, and the tracking system had pre-filled her name on the recommendation form as the highest-scoring finalist.

Then the written exercise was read properly. All three had answered the same question: Nishchay has 21.0 lakh policies in force and 6.3 lakh due this quarter; estimate the premium at risk and say where to intervene.

Nishtha's answer, in Exhibit 2, was a model of signposting: she comprehended, identified the customer, listed segments, evaluated and summarised. The segmentation step produced four at-risk flags, each counted across the whole book, and she added them — 7.4 plus 9.1 plus 4.2 plus 12.6, giving 33.3 lakh policies at risk, more than the 21.0 lakh that exist. She then multiplied by the ₹1,480 average premium and reported ₹492.84 crore at risk in one quarter, against a whole-year book of ₹310.8 crore. This case knows the figure is wrong; it is reproduced because the framework that produced it never caught it.

The flags overlap heavily: a policyholder whose agent has left is likely also a low-engagement one. On Nishchay's data, 11.8 lakh of the 21.0 lakh policies carry at least one flag, 56.2 per cent of the book. That prevalence applied to the renewal cohort gives 3.54 lakh of the 6.3 lakh policies due, again 56.2 per cent, and ₹52.39 crore at risk. Nishtha's figure was 9.4 times too large. No step in her framework asked whether the parts could exceed the whole.

Xavier's note ran 1,900 words, had no summary, and buried its estimate on page three: 3.4 lakh policies and about ₹50.32 crore, within four per cent of the reconciled figure. He got there by asking the recruiter for the flag overlap before starting, and he alone wrote that the grace period made the lapse dashboard misleading. He ranked none of his five interventions.

Three beliefs held on 14 October had since come apart. Xavier was not late: his note was quarantined on 12 October and released on 14 October. Nishtha's figure was not a typo; invited to revisit it, she defended the method. And the Exhibit 4 split, read by the panel as evidence that framework fluency predicts quality, was re-run on 17 October by Nurul Hashim, who noted that the rubric awards a fifth of the score for naming a framework, so the split largely measures itself. Exhibit 3, the only evidence Nishchay had about what its interviews predict, was at once the most interesting and the weakest document in the pack.

5. The people

Nilanjana Sheth, Director of Product, Mumbai, owns persistency against a board target of a 3 percentage point renewal improvement by March. She is not saying that she argued for the rubric in 2024 and now thinks it measures the wrong thing, which makes any exception look like an admission.

Xerxes Doctor, founder and chief executive, Mumbai, signs exceptions and speaks of the rubric as the thing that professionalised the company. He has not said that he renewed the consultancy contract personally in April, through March 2028.

Nachiket Dharap, Head of Engineering, Bengaluru, scored Nishtha 5 on Structure and Xavier 2. He wants a counterpart who can hold a roadmap conversation at speed; his team has lost two sprints to unclear requirements. He has not mentioned interviewing Xavier at 8.30 p.m. after an incident.

Niels Aartsen, Design Lead, Amsterdam, scored Xavier 5 on customer insight and Nishtha 4. Xavier alone described a real policyholder rather than a persona. He is not saying that he has twice been overruled on hiring, and is keeping count.

Njeri Wambui, Customer Success Lead, Nairobi, wants the hire on the Kenyan pilot, 2 per cent of revenue and all of her mandate. She rated Nishtha higher for asking about Kenya; she does not say she raised it.

Nuno Peixoto, Head of Partnerships, Lisbon, wants only that the renewals API ships before his brokers' January planning cycle, and backs whoever starts soonest. He has not told the panel that one broker contract, worth ₹2.9 crore a year, carries a February milestone.

Niyati Chokshi, Talent Lead, Ahmedabad, built Exhibit 4 and is measured on time-to-fill, now 73 days against a target of 55. She has not said that the search firm's fee is payable on Nishtha and not on Xavier, who applied directly.

Nurul Hashim, Senior Data Scientist, Kuala Lumpur, compiled Exhibit 3. She thinks eight rated hires settle nothing and has said so in writing. She also wants the rubric scrapped, which she argued for before she saw the data.

7. Voices

"She is the only one who did not make me do the work. Twenty minutes in, I knew where she was going and why. That is what I need at eleven at night when a release is breaking."
